quizzes.title: Problem-Solving Score Check
quizzes.description: Predict how a raw Problem-Solving Score reads as a band and what the score actually tracks.

questions.prompt: What increases a profile's Problem-Solving Score?

options.text: Any submission attempt, pass or fail
Only submissions that pass the challenge's test cases
Time spent logged into the platform

questions.explanation: Score only grows from challenges that actually pass their test cases — failed attempts don't contribute.

questions.prompt: A profile has a high Problem-Solving score and a zero SQL score. What does that mean?

options.text: Score is domain-scoped — strength in one domain says nothing about another
The SQL score will automatically rise to match

questions.explanation: Score accumulates per domain independently; a high score in one domain has no bearing on any other domain.

questions.prompt: Using bands beginner (<40), intermediate (40-69), advanced (>=70), what band is a score of exactly 40?

options.text: Undefined — 40 is a boundary with no band

questions.explanation: 40 is the first value in the intermediate band, since beginner only covers values strictly below 40.

questions.prompt: Which practice pattern tends to raise a domain score faster overall?

options.text: Solving one very Hard challenge and stopping
Consistent practice across many challenges of varying difficulty
Re-submitting the same passed challenge repeatedly

questions.explanation: Steady, broad practice compounds score gains faster than chasing a single high-difficulty win.

questions.prompt: Why use score bands (beginner/intermediate/advanced) instead of the raw number?

options.text: Bands are an official HackerRank feature that replaces the score
Bands make a large range of raw numbers easier to triage at a glance
Raw scores are not visible on profiles
Bands are required to unlock certifications

questions.explanation: Bands are a practical heuristic for quick triage, not an official HackerRank tiering system.

quizzes.title: Certifications Check
quizzes.description: Predict how a certification attempt outcome maps to what shows up on a profile.

questions.prompt: How is a HackerRank Skill Certification attempt graded?

options.text: As a percentage score shown publicly on the profile
As a binary pass/fail outcome for the whole attempt
By the number of certifications already earned

questions.explanation: A certification attempt has one outcome: pass or fail as a whole, based on a minimum threshold.

questions.prompt: What does the public profile show after a failed certification attempt?

options.text: Nothing new — only passed attempts become visible badges

questions.explanation: Failed attempts aren't displayed publicly; only a passed attempt produces a certificate badge.

questions.prompt: Why is a certification considered a stronger signal than a self-reported skill?

options.text: It's timed and proctored, making it harder to fake
It contributes directly to the Problem-Solving Score
It replaces the need for practice challenges

questions.explanation: The timed, proctored conditions make a passed certification a verified claim rather than a self-reported one.

questions.prompt: A candidate re-attempts a certification after failing once, and passes the second time. What shows on the profile?

options.text: Two badges, one marked failed and one passed
One badge, from the passed attempt
No badge, because one attempt failed
A badge only after a third attempt

questions.explanation: Only the passed outcome produces a badge; the earlier failed attempt leaves no public trace.

questions.prompt: Does passing a JavaScript certification change a profile's SQL score?

options.text: Yes, certifications add points to every related domain score
No, certifications and domain practice scores are independent
Only if the SQL score is already above intermediate
Yes, but only for Advanced-level certifications

questions.explanation: Certifications are a separate signal from domain practice scores — passing one doesn't move the other.

quizzes.title: Badges Check
quizzes.description: Predict how earned/total progress maps to a badge tier's status.

questions.prompt: What does a HackerRank skill badge track?

options.text: Cumulative solved-challenge count in a practice track

questions.explanation: Badges accumulate progress from solved challenges in a domain track over time, not from one attempt.

questions.prompt: A badge tier shows earned = 19, total = 20. What is its status?
questions.explanation: Status is only complete when earned equals total exactly; 19/20 is still in-progress.

questions.prompt: What happens once earned reaches total for a badge tier?

options.text: The badge is complete and progress resets toward the next tier
The badge disappears from the profile
You must retake a proctored test to keep it

questions.explanation: Completing a tier resets the progress counters toward the next, higher tier of the same badge.

questions.prompt: Unlike certifications, badges have no...
questions.explanation: Badges only track progress toward completion; there is no fail outcome the way a certification attempt has one.

questions.prompt: A badge progress fraction should always be printed as:
questions.explanation: The convention is earned first, then total, separated by a slash, regardless of completion status.

quizzes.title: Global Ranking Check
quizzes.description: Predict how a numeric rank maps to a tier, and what drives rank in the first place.

questions.prompt: What primarily drives a HackerRank global rank number?
questions.explanation: Rank is computed mostly from rated contest performance, not from untimed practice activity.

questions.prompt: Which rank is the stronger signal: #57 or #15234?

options.text: #15234, because higher numbers mean more points
#57, because a smaller rank number is better
Neither — rank has no meaningful ordering

questions.explanation: Rank works opposite to score: a lower number means a stronger relative standing.

questions.prompt: Using top-100 (<=100), top-1000 (<=1000), open (else), what tier is rank exactly 1000?
questions.explanation: 1000 is inclusive in the top-1000 band since it satisfies rank <= 1000 while being greater than 100.

questions.prompt: Why might a profile with lots of practice challenges solved have no meaningful contest rank?

options.text: Practice challenges don't feed into the rated contest rank
Rank is disabled for profiles with a high score
Practice and rank use the same formula, so this can't happen

questions.explanation: Rank is tied to rated contest participation, so untimed practice alone doesn't necessarily produce a meaningful rank.

questions.prompt: Most active users fall into the `open` tier. What does that imply?

options.text: Landing in `open` is expected and not, by itself, a weak signal

questions.explanation: The top tiers are narrow bands by design — most users, including strong ones, fall into the broad open range.

quizzes.title: Interview Preparation Kit Check
quizzes.description: Predict how the IPK organizes practice and which track a topic keyword should route to.

questions.prompt: How does the Interview Preparation Kit organize its problems?

options.text: By topic, so you can practice one recurring pattern at a time
Randomly, to simulate a real OA
By company that requested the problems

questions.explanation: IPK groups problems by topic (Arrays, Strings, DP, ...) so each session reinforces one pattern.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the `Warmup` set inside IPK?

options.text: The hardest problems, reserved for experts
The easiest entry problems, meant to build momentum
A random mix of every topic

questions.explanation: Warmup problems are intentionally easy — they exist to build momentum, not to test depth.

questions.prompt: If you're weak specifically on array manipulation, what's the most efficient next step?

options.text: Work through the kit strictly top-to-bottom regardless of topic
Route directly into the Arrays track
Repeat the Warmup set until it feels easy
Skip IPK entirely and take a certification instead

questions.explanation: IPK's topic-first structure lets you target a known weak spot directly instead of grinding unrelated problems.

questions.prompt: A topic keyword doesn't match `arrays`, `strings`, or `warmup`. What should a topic router do?

options.text: Throw an error — only three topics are valid
Route it into a general/mixed catch-all bucket

questions.explanation: Unrecognized topics fall into a general/mixed bucket by design rather than failing outright.

questions.prompt: Why does IPK organize practice by topic instead of by difficulty like score bands do?

options.text: Topic and difficulty are the same thing on HackerRank
Focused, pattern-based practice targets specific interview weaknesses better than a difficulty sort
Difficulty sorting is not possible in IPK
IPK doesn't allow you to see problem difficulty

questions.explanation: Interview prep benefits from reinforcing one recurring pattern at a time, which topic grouping enables and difficulty grouping doesn't.

quizzes.title: Online Assessments (OA) Check
quizzes.description: Predict how remaining time in a fixed OA window should change your pacing strategy.

questions.prompt: What is a defining trait of a HackerRank-hosted Online Assessment (OA)?

options.text: It can be paused and resumed at any time
It runs inside one fixed time window that typically can't be paused
It has no time limit at all

questions.explanation: OAs run against a single countdown for the whole session, usually without the ability to pause.

questions.prompt: With thresholds rush (<15 min), pace (<45 min), plan (>=45 min), what mode applies at exactly 45 minutes remaining?
questions.explanation: 45 minutes is the first value that reaches the plan threshold, since pace only covers values strictly below 45.

questions.prompt: Why does pacing mode change as time runs out during an OA?

options.text: Because effort should stay proportional to time remaining, favoring partial credit late on
Because later questions are always easier
Pacing mode has no real effect on outcome

questions.explanation: Treating minute 5 like minute 80 wastes the fixed clock; late-window strategy should favor banking partial credit.

questions.prompt: In `rush` mode with a question you can't fully solve, what's the recommended move?

options.text: Submit whatever passes the most visible test cases for partial credit
Wait for the timer to expire

questions.explanation: Since grading is per test case, submitting a partial solution still banks credit even under time pressure.

questions.prompt: Does the rush/pace/plan idea only apply to HackerRank OAs specifically?

options.text: No, it generalizes to any timed, multi-question test with a fixed window
Yes, it only works for coding questions, never multiple choice
No, it only applies to certifications

questions.explanation: The pacing strategy is a general timed-test tactic, not something specific to HackerRank's implementation.

quizzes.title: Implementation Focus Check
quizzes.description: Predict what an implementation checklist's done/todo counts actually tell you.

questions.prompt: What usually causes lost points on an "Implementation"-tagged problem?

options.text: Choosing an algorithm with the wrong time complexity
Missing one of the spec's rules, not picking a bad algorithm
Submitting too early in the OA window

questions.explanation: Implementation problems are about completeness — most lost points come from an unhandled rule in the statement.

questions.prompt: In a checklist line like `[x] parse input`, what does the `[x]` marker mean?

options.text: The rule has been marked done
The rule caused a runtime error

questions.explanation: `[x]` at the start of a line marks that requirement as completed; `[ ]` marks it as still open.

questions.prompt: A checklist shows `done=5 todo=0` but a hidden test still fails. What does that most likely mean?

options.text: A "done" item was marked complete but implemented incorrectly
Hidden tests never relate to the spec
The checklist format itself caused the failure

questions.explanation: "Done" tracks completeness of coverage, not correctness — a covered rule can still be implemented wrong.

questions.prompt: Why does a checklist mindset fit implementation problems specifically?

options.text: Because these problems need a clever algorithm above all
Because success depends on covering every stated rule, which a checklist tracks well
Because HackerRank requires a literal checklist in the submission
Because checklists are faster to type than code

questions.explanation: Implementation problems reward completeness over cleverness, which is exactly what a rule-by-rule checklist verifies.

questions.prompt: Which line(s) count as free-form notes rather than checklist items, for counting purposes?

options.text: Any line not starting with `[x]` or `[ ]`
All lines are checklist items regardless of format

questions.explanation: Only lines that start with the exact `[x]` or `[ ]` markers are counted; everything else is ignored as non-checklist content.

quizzes.title: Test Case Handling Check
quizzes.description: Predict which edge-case categories a given set of flags exercises.

questions.prompt: How does HackerRank typically grade a submission?

options.text: Per test case, awarding partial credit
By comparing runtime against other submitters

questions.explanation: Grading is per test case — a submission can pass some hidden cases and fail others, earning partial credit.

questions.prompt: Why do hidden test cases often target inputs like zero or a single element?

options.text: To slow down the judge on purpose
Because general-case logic quietly breaks on these boundary inputs
Because they're easier to write than normal cases
They're only used in certification tests, never regular problems

questions.explanation: Boundary inputs like zero, negative, empty, or single-element frequently expose assumptions baked into general-case code.

questions.prompt: Why can a truthy check like `if (value)` silently break on a numeric edge case?

options.text: Because `0` is falsy, so a valid zero value gets treated as absent
Because truthy checks always throw on numbers
Because negative numbers are always truthy
Truthy checks never cause issues with numbers

questions.explanation: `0` is falsy in JavaScript, so code guarding on truthiness can wrongly treat a legitimate zero as missing data.

questions.prompt: Given the input line `neg empty zero`, sorted alphabetically, what should be printed?
questions.explanation: Alphabetical order of {empty, neg, zero} is empty, neg, zero — regardless of the order tokens arrived in.

questions.prompt: If none of the four known flags (`empty`, `zero`, `neg`, `single`) appear in the input, what should be printed?
questions.explanation: The literal word `none` is the defined output when no recognized edge-case category is present.

lessons.title: System Design (Scalability, CAP Theorem)
lessons.markdown:
# System Design (Scalability, CAP Theorem)

> Graph index: `07.1`

<!-- cursor:teacher:add-explanation (deterministic) -->
<!-- marker:javascript/07-technical-interview-preparation/07.1-system-design-scalability-cap-theorem:README.md -->

## Context

Junior/mid interviews rarely ask for a full distributed-systems design, but they often probe whether you can **reason about trade-offs** at a high level: "what happens when this gets 10x traffic?", "what if the database node goes down?". The **CAP theorem** is the compact vocabulary interviewers expect: a distributed system can only guarantee two of **Consistency**, **Availability**, and **Partition tolerance** at the same time.

- **Consistency (C)** — every read sees the latest write (or an error).
- **Availability (A)** — every request gets a (non-error) response, even if it's not the latest data.
- **Partition tolerance (P)** — the system keeps working when nodes can't talk to each other.

In real systems, network partitions **will** happen, so the practical choice is between **CP** (favor consistency, reject/queue requests during a partition) and **AP** (favor availability, serve possibly-stale data during a partition). **CA** only exists in the theoretical case of no partitions — in practice, choosing "CA" means you have **not actually planned for a partition**.

## Predict first

An interviewer says: "Our payments ledger must never show two different balances to two different users during a network split, even if that means some requests time out." Which guarantee is being **sacrificed**, and which pair (CP/AP/CA) does this system land in?

## Explanation

Map each pair to the guarantee it gives up when a partition happens:

| Pair | Keeps | Sacrifices | Typical use case |
|------|-------|------------|-------------------|
| **CP** | Consistency + Partition tolerance | **Availability** — some requests fail or block during a split | Payments, inventory counts, anything where stale data is worse than an error |
| **AP** | Availability + Partition tolerance | **Consistency** — reads may return stale data during a split | Social feeds, product catalogs, shopping carts, presence/"online" indicators |
| **CA** | Consistency + Availability | **Partition tolerance** — assumes the network never splits | Single-node databases, or a claim that doesn't survive real distributed conditions |

The payments example above is **CP**: it explicitly accepts failed/timed-out requests (giving up **availability**) to guarantee every visible balance is correct.

The interview move that matters is not memorizing the table — it's **naming the trade-off out loud**: "I'm choosing CP here because a stale balance is a business risk we can't accept; a slow response is more tolerable."

## What to observe

- CAP is about behavior **during a network partition**, not normal operation — most of the time C and A both hold.
- "CA" is a red flag in an interview answer unless you explicitly justify why partitions are impossible (e.g., single machine, no replicas).
- Naming the **sacrificed** guarantee is more useful to an interviewer than naming the two you keep — it shows you understand the cost.
- Scalability questions ("what if traffic 10x's?") often hide a CAP question underneath ("what if the cache/replica falls behind?").

## Quick challenge

For each scenario, say which pair (CP/AP/CA) fits and which guarantee is sacrificed — then justify it in one sentence, the way you would out loud in an interview:

1. A live sports score ticker that must never go down, even if some viewers see a score that's a few seconds old.
2. A bank transfer service that must refuse a transfer rather than risk double-spending during a network split.

lessons.title: Behavioral (STAR Method)
lessons.markdown:
# Behavioral (STAR Method)

> Graph index: `07.2`

<!-- cursor:teacher:add-explanation (deterministic) -->
<!-- marker:javascript/07-technical-interview-preparation/07.2-behavioral-star-method:README.md -->

## Context

Behavioral questions ("Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate") are graded on **structure**, not just content. The **STAR method** gives you that structure:

- **Situation** — the context: where, when, what was at stake.
- **Task** — your specific responsibility or goal in that situation.
- **Action** — what **you** concretely did (not "we").
- **Result** — the measurable or observable outcome, ideally with a number or a lesson learned.

Answers that skip **Task** or **Action** tend to sound like vague stories. Answers that skip **Result** leave the interviewer wondering if it worked.

## Predict first

A candidate answers: "Our team's deploy pipeline kept failing. I looked into it and eventually it got fixed." Which STAR letters are **missing**, and why does this answer feel incomplete?

## Explanation

That answer has a **Situation** (failing pipeline) but is missing a clear **Task** (was fixing it your responsibility, or did you volunteer?), a concrete **Action** ("I looked into it" is not specific — what did you actually do?), and a measurable **Result** ("eventually it got fixed" — by whom, how, how long, what changed?).

A stronger version:

- **Situation**: "Our deploy pipeline had a 30% failure rate for two weeks, blocking releases."
- **Task**: "As the on-call engineer, I was asked to find the root cause."
- **Action**: "I added logging around the flaky step, found a race condition in a cache warm-up script, and rewrote it to wait on a readiness check."
- **Result**: "Failure rate dropped to under 2%, and releases went from twice a week back to daily."

Notice each letter answers a **different question**: Situation = context, Task = your job, Action = your verbs, Result = the number/outcome.

## What to observe

- A complete STAR answer names all four parts explicitly, even briefly — don't let Action blur into Situation.
- **Action** should use "I", not "we" — the interviewer wants to know your specific contribution.
- **Result** is stronger with a concrete measure (percentage, time saved, count) or a clearly stated lesson.
- Vague verbs ("looked into it", "helped out") are a sign the Action step needs more detail.

## Quick challenge

Take this rough story and sort it into the four STAR labels, rewriting each line to be concrete: "There was a bug in production. I was the one who had to fix it since I wrote that code. I read the logs, found the null check was missing, added it, and shipped a hotfix. After that, the crash reports stopped completely."

lessons.title: Communication and Clarifying Questions
lessons.markdown:
# Communication and Clarifying Questions

> Graph index: `07.3`

<!-- cursor:teacher:add-explanation (deterministic) -->
<!-- marker:javascript/07-technical-interview-preparation/07.3-communication-and-clarifying-questions:README.md -->

## Context

Interviewers deliberately leave coding prompts **underspecified** — "write a function that merges two lists" hides questions about duplicates, order, size limits, and input types. Jumping straight to code without asking is one of the most common ways strong coders lose points. A good clarifying question does two things: it removes a real ambiguity, and it signals what you're already thinking about (constraints, edge cases, example shapes).

## Predict first

A prompt says: "Write a function that returns the top K most frequent words in a list." Before writing any code, list at least three clarifying questions you would ask. Then compare: do your questions target **constraints** (input size, case sensitivity) or just restate the problem?

## Explanation

Weak clarifying questions restate the prompt ("so I need the top K words?") — they don't reduce ambiguity. Strong clarifying questions target concrete unknowns:

- **Constraints**: "What's the expected size of the input list — could it be millions of words?" "Should word comparison be case-sensitive?"
- **Ties**: "If two words have the same frequency, does order matter?"
- **Example**: "Can you confirm — for `["a","b","a"]` with K=1, the answer is `["a"]`?"

Notice the pattern: each good question either narrows a **constraint** (size, case, format) or checks understanding with a concrete **example**. Asking "can you give me an example input/output?" is often the single highest-value question, because it exposes assumptions on both sides immediately.

## What to observe

- A question that just repeats the prompt back doesn't move the conversation forward — target specifics (limits, ties, formats, edge cases).
- Confirming a concrete example ("so for `X` the output would be `Y`, correct?") catches misunderstandings before you write a single line of code.
- Asking too many questions before showing any thinking can stall — pair questions with a brief statement of your working assumption ("I'll assume case-insensitive unless you say otherwise").
- Narrating your assumptions out loud is a form of communication even when you don't ask a literal question.

## Quick challenge

For the prompt "Write a function that checks if a string is a palindrome," write two clarifying questions: one about a **constraint** (e.g., case, spaces, punctuation) and one that proposes a concrete **example** for the interviewer to confirm.

lessons.title: Code Quality and Maintainability
Iterative Optimization
lessons.markdown:
# Iterative Optimization

> Graph index: `07.5`

<!-- cursor:teacher:add-explanation (deterministic) -->
<!-- marker:javascript/07-technical-interview-preparation/07.5-iterative-optimization:README.md -->

## Context

Most coding interviews expect you to **narrate improvement**, not jump straight to the optimal solution. The typical arc is: get a **brute force** solution working first (even if slow), then talk through a **better** approach, then reach for the **optimal** one — explaining the complexity gain at each step. Interviewers weight this narration heavily: silently writing an optimal solution with no explanation often scores lower than talking through the same journey out loud.

## Predict first

For "find the two numbers in an array that sum to a target," what's the brute-force approach, what complexity does it have, and what single data structure gets you to the optimal approach? Answer before reading on.

## Explanation

- **Brute force**: check every pair with nested loops. Complexity **O(n²)** — correct, but slow for large inputs.
- **Better**: sort the array first, then use two pointers moving inward. Complexity **O(n log n)** — the sort dominates, but it's a real improvement and shows you know sorting unlocks two-pointer techniques.
- **Optimal**: use a hash map to record numbers seen so far; for each number, check if `target - number` was already seen. Complexity **O(n)** — one pass, constant-time lookups.

The narration matters as much as the code: "I'll start with the brute-force nested loop to make sure I understand the problem — that's O(n²). Then I'll improve it with a hash map to get to O(n), trading some space for time." Saying the complexity **out loud** at each step is exactly what interviewers listen for.

## What to observe

- Brute force → better → optimal is a narration pattern, not just a coding pattern — say the complexity at each step.
- "Better" doesn't have to be the theoretical best — showing an intermediate improvement (like sorting) demonstrates incremental thinking.
- The jump from O(n²) to O(n) often comes from trading space for time (e.g., a hash map) — name that trade-off explicitly.
- Landing directly on the optimal solution with no narration can score lower than talking through brute force → better → optimal, even if the final code is identical.

## Quick challenge

For "check if a string has any repeated characters," describe a brute-force approach and its complexity, then describe an optimal approach and its complexity. Name the data structure that gets you there.

# CAP Trade-off Labeler

## Problem context

During a system design discussion, an interviewer names a trade-off (CP, AP, or CA) and expects you to instantly name **what it costs**. A quick CLI drill turns that recall into muscle memory: given the pair, name the sacrificed guarantee.

## Goal

Read one line from stdin containing `CP`, `AP`, or `CA` and print the single guarantee that pair sacrifices during a network partition: `availability`, `consistency`, or `partition-tolerance`.

## Lesson concepts practiced
- [ ] CP keeps Consistency + Partition tolerance and sacrifices Availability
- [ ] AP keeps Availability + Partition tolerance and sacrifices Consistency
- [ ] CA assumes no partitions, so it sacrifices Partition tolerance
- [ ] Naming the sacrificed guarantee (not the two kept) is the useful interview signal

## Functional requirements
- [ ] Read exactly one line from stdin containing `CP`, `AP`, or `CA`
- [ ] Print `availability` when the line is `CP`
- [ ] Print `consistency` when the line is `AP`
- [ ] Print `partition-tolerance` when the line is `CA`
- [ ] Output is a single line ending with a newline

## Non-functional requirements
- [ ] Readability and maintainability: a single lookup table/map, no chained `if/else` per branch duplicated
- [ ] Error handling: unrecognized input may throw or print an error (no special requirement)
- [ ] Performance (when applicable): O(1) lookup, trivial for this input size

## Constraints
- [ ] Node.js only — no external libraries
- [ ] Input is exactly one of the three uppercase pairs: `CP`, `AP`, `CA`
- [ ] Do not hardcode all logic as three separate `if` blocks with repeated `console.log` calls — prefer a map/lookup keyed by the pair

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] stdin `CP` → stdout `availability`
- [ ] stdin `AP` → stdout `consistency`
- [ ] stdin `CA` → stdout `partition-tolerance`
- [ ] Output has no extra text before or after the single guarantee word

## Example data

Input:
```text
CP
```

Output:
```text
availability
```

Input:
```text
AP
```

Output:
```text
consistency
```

## Suggested plan (no solution)
1. Read the single stdin line and trim it.
2. Build a lookup object mapping `CP` → `availability`, `AP` → `consistency`, `CA` → `partition-tolerance`.
3. Print the looked-up value followed by a newline.

## Deliverables
- [ ] Code in `starter/` (`index.js` scaffold + `tests.json` validation cases + `sample.input` example stdin)
- [ ] (Optional) reference in `solution/`

## Extensions (optional)
- [ ] Accept lowercase input (`cp`, `ap`, `ca`) by normalizing case before lookup
- [ ] Print a one-sentence justification alongside the guarantee (e.g. "availability — some requests fail during a split")

# STAR Answer Formatter

## Problem context

Before a behavioral interview, candidates often jot down four rough lines for a story. A formatter that labels each line clearly (`Situation:`, `Task:`, `Action:`, `Result:`) makes it obvious at a glance whether any part is missing or too short.

## Goal

Read exactly four lines from stdin, in order (Situation, Task, Action, Result), and print each one prefixed with its STAR label.

## Lesson concepts practiced
- [ ] A complete STAR answer names all four parts explicitly: Situation, Task, Action, Result
- [ ] Each STAR letter answers a different question (context, responsibility, concrete steps, measurable outcome)
- [ ] Labeling each part makes it easy to spot when one is missing or too vague

## Functional requirements
- [ ] Read exactly 4 lines from stdin, in this fixed order: Situation, Task, Action, Result
- [ ] Print 4 output lines, each formatted as `<Label>: <text>` using the labels `Situation`, `Task`, `Action`, `Result`
- [ ] Preserve the original text of each line exactly (aside from trimming trailing whitespace/newline)
- [ ] Print the 4 labeled lines in the same S/T/A/R order they were read

## Non-functional requirements
- [ ] Readability and maintainability: pair labels with input lines using a single array of label names, not four repeated `console.log` statements with hardcoded strings
- [ ] Error handling: fewer than 4 lines may produce fewer labeled lines (no special requirement)
- [ ] Performance (when applicable): trivial for 4 lines of input

## Constraints
- [ ] Node.js only — no external libraries
- [ ] Input is always 4 lines, one STAR component per line, in S/T/A/R order
- [ ] Do not reorder or reword the input text — only add the label prefix

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] 4 lines `Pipeline kept failing`, `Find and fix the root cause`, `Added logging, found a race condition, rewrote the warm-up script`, `Failure rate dropped from 30% to under 2%` → 4 labeled output lines in that order
- [ ] Output line 1 starts with `Situation: `
- [ ] Output line 2 starts with `Task: `
- [ ] Output line 3 starts with `Action: `
- [ ] Output line 4 starts with `Result: `

## Example data

Input:
```text
Pipeline kept failing
Find and fix the root cause
Added logging, found a race condition, rewrote the warm-up script
Failure rate dropped from 30% to under 2%
```

Output:
```text
Situation: Pipeline kept failing
Task: Find and fix the root cause
Action: Added logging, found a race condition, rewrote the warm-up script
Result: Failure rate dropped from 30% to under 2%
```

## Suggested plan (no solution)
1. Read all stdin lines into an array.
2. Define the label order: `["Situation", "Task", "Action", "Result"]`.
3. Pair each label with the corresponding input line (by index) and format as `<Label>: <text>`.
4. Print each formatted line, one per line.

## Deliverables
- [ ] Code in `starter/` (`index.js` scaffold + `tests.json` validation cases + `sample.input` example stdin)
- [ ] (Optional) reference in `solution/`

## Extensions (optional)
- [ ] Print a warning line if any of the 4 lines is empty or shorter than a few words
- [ ] Support an optional 5th line and label it `Reflection:`

projects.title: 001. Clarify Gate
projects.readmeMarkdown:
# Clarify Gate

## Problem context

Before diving into code, a candidate should ask questions that target real ambiguities — constraints or concrete examples — not just restate the prompt. A quick automated check can flag whether a list of jotted-down questions clears that bar before the interview starts.

## Goal

Read lines from stdin until end of input, treating each line as one clarifying question. Print `ready` if the questions clear the bar, otherwise print `ask-more`.

## Lesson concepts practiced
- [ ] A clarifying question should target a real ambiguity, not restate the prompt
- [ ] Constraint questions (size, case, format, ties) and example-confirmation questions are the highest-value question types
- [ ] Checking for at least one real question mark and one constraint/example keyword is a simple proxy for "did the candidate ask something useful"

## Functional requirements
- [ ] Read every line from stdin until EOF; each line is one candidate question or note
- [ ] Print `ready` if **both** conditions hold: at least one line contains a `?` character, **and** at least one line contains the word `constraint` or `example` (case-insensitive, substring match)
- [ ] Print `ask-more` if either condition fails
- [ ] Print exactly one output line (`ready` or `ask-more`)

## Non-functional requirements
- [ ] Readability and maintainability: compute the two boolean conditions separately, then combine them, rather than one large nested condition
- [ ] Error handling: empty input (zero lines) should print `ask-more`
- [ ] Performance (when applicable): a single pass over the lines is sufficient

## Constraints
- [ ] Node.js only — no external libraries
- [ ] Matching for `constraint`/`example` must be case-insensitive (e.g. `Example`, `CONSTRAINT` count)
- [ ] The `?` check and the keyword check can be satisfied by different lines — they don't need to be on the same line

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Lines `What's the max input size?` and `Can you confirm an example output?` → stdout `ready`

# Smell Scanner

## Problem context

Before submitting a solution in an interview or a pull request, it helps to run a quick automated pass that flags obvious leftover debugging artifacts and legacy patterns, so you catch them before a human reviewer does.

## Goal

Read lines of code-like text from stdin until end of input and print `smell` if any line contains a flagged pattern, otherwise print `clean`.

## Lesson concepts practiced
- [ ] Leftover `console.log` calls are a maintainability smell even when the logic is correct
- [ ] Unresolved `TODO` comments signal a known, acknowledged gap left in submitted code
- [ ] `var` is a smell in modern JavaScript due to function-scoping and hoisting surprises

## Functional requirements
- [ ] Read every line from stdin until EOF; each line is one line of code-like text
- [ ] Print `smell` if **any** line matches the pattern `var ` (case-insensitive), `console.log` (case-insensitive), or `TODO` (case-insensitive)
- [ ] Print `clean` only if **no** line matches any of those patterns
- [ ] Print exactly one output line (`smell` or `clean`)

## Non-functional requirements
- [ ] Readability and maintainability: express the three patterns as a single regular expression or a small array of patterns, not three separate duplicated loops
- [ ] Error handling: empty input (zero lines) should print `clean`
- [ ] Performance (when applicable): a single pass over the lines is sufficient

## Constraints
- [ ] Node.js only — no external libraries
- [ ] The `var ` check requires a trailing space (so it matches `var x = 1` but not, say, the substring inside another word)
- [ ] Matching must be case-insensitive for all three patterns (e.g. `Console.log`, `TODO`, `Var x` all count)

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Lines `function total(items) {` and `var sum = 0;` → stdout `smell` (matches `var `)
- [ ] Lines `function greet(name) {` and `console.log(name);` → stdout `smell` (matches `console.log`)
- [ ] Lines `function add(a, b) {` and `// TODO: validate inputs` → stdout `smell` (matches `TODO`)
- [ ] Lines `const sum = a + b;` and `return sum;` (no flagged pattern) → stdout `clean`
- [ ] Empty stdin (no lines) → stdout `clean`

## Example data

Input:
```text
function total(items) {
var sum = 0;
console.log("debugging", items);
// TODO: handle empty array
return sum;
}
```

Output:
```text
smell
```

Input:
```text
function add(a, b) {
const sum = a + b;
return sum;
}
```

Output:
```text
clean
```

## Suggested plan (no solution)
1. Read all stdin lines into an array (may be empty).
2. Build one case-insensitive regular expression covering `var `, `console.log`, and `TODO`.
3. Check whether any line matches the regular expression.
4. Print `smell` if a match was found, otherwise print `clean`.

## Deliverables
- [ ] Code in `starter/` (`index.js` scaffold + `tests.json` validation cases + `sample.input` example stdin)
- [ ] (Optional) reference in `solution/`

## Extensions (optional)
- [ ] Print the 1-based line number of the first matching line alongside `smell`
- [ ] Also flag `debugger;` statements as a smell

projects.readmeMarkdown:
# Complexity Upgrade Labeler

## Problem context

Practicing the brute force → better → optimal narration is easier when you can instantly recall the complexity tag that goes with each stage. A quick CLI drill turns that recall into muscle memory before you have to say it out loud in an interview.

## Goal

Read one line from stdin containing `brute`, `better`, or `optimal` and print the target complexity tag associated with that narration stage: `O(n^2)`, `O(n log n)`, or `O(n)`.

## Lesson concepts practiced
- [ ] The brute-force stage of a solution is typically O(n^2) (e.g. nested loops checking every pair)
- [ ] The better stage often reaches O(n log n) (e.g. sorting first, then a linear scan)
- [ ] The optimal stage often reaches O(n) by trading space for time (e.g. a hash map)
- [ ] Naming the complexity out loud at each narration stage is what interviewers listen for

## Functional requirements
- [ ] Read exactly one line from stdin containing `brute`, `better`, or `optimal`
- [ ] Print `O(n^2)` when the line is `brute`
- [ ] Print `O(n log n)` when the line is `better`
- [ ] Print `O(n)` when the line is `optimal`
- [ ] Output is a single line ending with a newline

## Non-functional requirements
- [ ] Readability and maintainability: use a single lookup map keyed by stage name, not three duplicated `if` branches
- [ ] Error handling: unrecognized input may throw or print an error (no special requirement)
- [ ] Performance (when applicable): O(1) lookup, trivial for this input size

## Constraints
- [ ] Node.js only — no external libraries
- [ ] Input is exactly one of the three lowercase stage names: `brute`, `better`, `optimal`
- [ ] Print the complexity tags exactly as shown, including the `O(...)` notation and the caret-free `n^2` spelling

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] stdin `brute` → stdout `O(n^2)`
- [ ] stdin `better` → stdout `O(n log n)`
- [ ] stdin `optimal` → stdout `O(n)`
- [ ] Output has no extra text before or after the complexity tag

## Example data

Input:
```text
brute
```

Output:
```text
O(n^2)
```

Input:
```text
optimal
```

Output:
```text
O(n)
```

## Suggested plan (no solution)
1. Read the single stdin line and trim it.
2. Build a lookup object mapping `brute` → `O(n^2)`, `better` → `O(n log n)`, `optimal` → `O(n)`.
3. Print the looked-up value followed by a newline.

## Deliverables
- [ ] Code in `starter/` (`index.js` scaffold + `tests.json` validation cases + `sample.input` example stdin)
- [ ] (Optional) reference in `solution/`

## Extensions (optional)
- [ ] Accept a fourth stage `constant` that maps to `O(1)`
- [ ] Print a short one-sentence example technique alongside the tag (e.g. "O(n) — hash map, one pass")

quizzes.title: CAP Theorem Check
quizzes.description: Predict which guarantee a system sacrifices and classify CP/AP/CA scenarios.

questions.prompt: According to the CAP theorem, what can a distributed system guarantee during a network partition?

options.text: All three of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance at once
At most two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance
CAP only applies to single-node databases

questions.explanation: CAP theorem: when a partition occurs, a system can only keep two of the three guarantees — typically Consistency+Partition tolerance (CP) or Availability+Partition tolerance (AP).

questions.prompt: A payments ledger rejects/blocks some requests during a network split so that no user ever sees a stale balance. Which guarantee is sacrificed?
questions.explanation: This is a CP system: it keeps Consistency and Partition tolerance, giving up Availability (some requests fail or time out) during a split.

questions.prompt: A social media feed keeps responding during a network split, but some viewers may see slightly stale posts. Which pair does this describe?

options.text: None of the three; CAP does not apply to feeds

questions.explanation: Always responding (availability) while accepting possibly-stale reads (sacrificing consistency) during a partition is the AP trade-off.

questions.prompt: Why is claiming a distributed system is "CA" usually a red flag in an interview answer?

options.text: CA systems are always faster than CP or AP systems
CA assumes network partitions never happen, which is unrealistic for real distributed systems
CA is not a real combination described by CAP theorem
CA only applies to NoSQL databases

questions.explanation: In practice, partitions will happen. Claiming "CA" without justifying why partitions are impossible (e.g., a true single machine) signals the trade-off wasn't actually considered.

questions.prompt: What is the more interview-effective move when discussing a CAP trade-off: naming the two guarantees you keep, or naming the one you sacrifice?

options.text: Naming the two you keep — it sounds more positive
Naming the one you sacrifice, with a reason tied to the business risk
Neither matters — just say "CAP theorem" and move on
Avoid naming any guarantee and only discuss latency

questions.explanation: Naming the sacrificed guarantee and justifying it (e.g., "a stale balance is worse than a slow response here") demonstrates you understand the real cost of the choice.

questions.prompt: A live sports score ticker must never go down, even if some viewers briefly see an outdated score. Which guarantee is sacrificed?
questions.explanation: Staying up (availability) while tolerating stale scores (sacrificing consistency) during a partition is the AP trade-off — consistency is what's given up.

quizzes.title: STAR Method Check
quizzes.description: Predict what a complete STAR answer needs and spot missing parts.

questions.prompt: What do the four letters in STAR stand for?
questions.explanation: STAR = Situation (context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what you did), Result (the outcome).

questions.prompt: "Our deploy pipeline kept failing. I looked into it and eventually it got fixed." Which STAR part is weakest in this answer?

options.text: Action and Result — both are vague, with no specific steps or measurable outcome
Nothing is missing; this is a complete STAR answer
Task — the pipeline itself is the task

questions.explanation: "I looked into it" doesn't say what was actually done (Action), and "eventually it got fixed" gives no measurable outcome (Result).

questions.prompt: Why should the Action step use "I" instead of "we"?

options.text: Because teamwork should never be mentioned in interviews
Because the interviewer wants to know your specific, individual contribution
Because "we" is grammatically incorrect in behavioral answers
It doesn't matter which pronoun is used

questions.explanation: The interviewer is evaluating your individual impact. "We" can hide whether you personally did anything, so Action should be specific to your actions.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the strongest Result statement?

options.text: "It worked out fine in the end."
"The failure rate dropped from 30% to under 2%, and releases returned to a daily cadence."

questions.explanation: A strong Result gives a measurable before/after (percentages, counts, cadence) rather than a vague feeling.

questions.prompt: What role does the Task step play in a STAR answer?

options.text: It restates the Situation in different words
It clarifies what your specific responsibility or goal was in that situation
It is optional and can always be skipped
It describes the final measurable outcome

questions.explanation: Task answers "what was I responsible for / trying to achieve" — distinct from the context (Situation) and the steps taken (Action).

questions.prompt: A candidate says: "There was a bug. I fixed it. Great." What is the biggest structural problem with this as a STAR answer?

options.text: Every part (S, T, A, R) is too vague to show real context, responsibility, concrete steps, or measurable outcome

questions.explanation: Each STAR letter needs enough concrete detail to answer its specific question; this answer is too compressed to show any of the four parts clearly.

quizzes.title: Clarifying Questions Check
quizzes.description: Predict which clarifying questions actually reduce ambiguity before coding.

questions.prompt: Why do interviewers often leave coding prompts underspecified on purpose?

options.text: To see whether the candidate asks questions that surface real ambiguities before coding
Because writing a fully specified prompt is too much work
Underspecified prompts are always a mistake and should be reported
So candidates are forced to guess without asking anything

questions.explanation: Ambiguity is often intentional — it tests whether the candidate identifies and resolves unknowns (constraints, edge cases) before diving into code.

questions.prompt: "So I need to find the top K most frequent words, right?" — what's the main problem with this as a clarifying question?

options.text: It restates the prompt without reducing any real ambiguity
It should not use the word "words"
Nothing — this is a strong clarifying question

questions.explanation: Restating the prompt doesn't narrow any unknown (size, ties, case sensitivity) — a strong question targets a specific constraint or example.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the strongest clarifying question for "top K most frequent words"?

options.text: "If two words tie in frequency, does the order between them matter?"

questions.explanation: This targets a concrete ambiguity (tie-breaking behavior) that changes the correct implementation — a real constraint, not a restatement.

questions.prompt: Why is confirming a concrete example ("for `["a","b","a"]` with K=1, the answer is `["a"]`, correct?") often the highest-value question?

options.text: It wastes time the interviewer would rather spend elsewhere
It exposes mismatched assumptions on both sides before any code is written
Examples are never useful in interviews
It replaces the need for any other clarifying question

questions.explanation: A concrete example forces both sides to agree on input/output shape and edge-case behavior immediately, catching misunderstandings early.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you decide not to ask about every possible ambiguity before starting?

options.text: Say nothing and hope the interviewer doesn't notice
State your working assumption out loud (e.g., "I'll assume case-insensitive unless told otherwise")
Always ask every possible question, no matter how many
Refuse to start coding until every ambiguity is resolved

questions.explanation: Narrating an assumption is a form of communication that keeps momentum while still surfacing your reasoning to the interviewer.

questions.prompt: Which pair of question types does the lesson identify as most likely to reduce real ambiguity?

options.text: Questions about constraints and questions that propose a concrete example
Questions about the interviewer's mood and the room temperature
Questions that simply repeat the prompt word for word
Questions about unrelated topics to build rapport

questions.explanation: Constraint questions (size, case, ties, format) and example-confirmation questions both target concrete unknowns rather than restating the prompt.

quizzes.title: Code Quality Check
quizzes.description: Predict which patterns count as code smells and why they matter for maintainability.

questions.prompt: A function works correctly on the happy path but still has a leftover `console.log("debugging", items)` call. Is this a code smell worth flagging?

options.text: No — if the logic is correct, nothing else matters
Yes — debug output left in shipped code pollutes logs and signals the code wasn't cleaned up
No — console.log is always required for production debugging
Only if the function also throws an error

questions.explanation: Code smells are about maintainability risk, not just correctness on the happy path. Leftover debug logging is a classic sign of incomplete cleanup.

questions.prompt: Why is `var` considered a smell in modern JavaScript, even in code that currently works?

options.text: `var` is function-scoped and hoisted, which can leak variables and enable rebinding bugs that `let`/`const` prevent
`var` was removed from the language and no longer works

questions.explanation: `var`'s function scoping and hoisting create surprises that `let`/`const` avoid via block scoping and the temporal dead zone.

questions.prompt: What does a `// TODO: handle empty array` comment signal to a code reviewer?

options.text: The author already handled every edge case perfectly
The author is aware of a known gap that was left unresolved before this code was submitted
TODOs are purely decorative and carry no information
The function will throw an error immediately

questions.explanation: A TODO comment documents a known, acknowledged gap — useful for tracking, but a smell if it's left in code being reviewed as "done."

questions.prompt: When flagging a code smell in review, what should accompany the flag?

options.text: Nothing — just say "this is bad" and move on
A one-sentence reason for what could go wrong later, not just a style preference
A demand to rewrite the entire file from scratch
A link to an unrelated style guide with no explanation

questions.explanation: Naming the concrete risk (e.g., "empty array silently returns 0, which might be wrong") is more persuasive and educational than a bare style objection.

questions.prompt: A snippet has correct logic but includes `var`, a leftover `console.log`, and an unresolved `TODO`. How many maintainability smells does this contain?

options.text: Zero — correct logic means no smells
One — only the most severe issue counts
Three — `var`, `console.log`, and `TODO` are each independent smells
It's impossible to have more than one smell in the same function

questions.explanation: Each pattern is an independent maintainability risk; a snippet can have multiple smells simultaneously even if it runs correctly.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the difference between a "bug" and a "code smell"?

options.text: A bug means the code produces a wrong result now; a smell is a maintainability risk that may not affect correctness today
They mean exactly the same thing
A smell always means the tests will fail
A bug is always caused by a code smell

questions.explanation: Code smells (leftover logs, TODOs, var) don't necessarily break the happy path — that's exactly why they're easy to miss and worth flagging anyway.

quizzes.title: Iterative Optimization Check
quizzes.description: Predict the complexity tag for brute force, better, and optimal narration steps.

questions.prompt: For "find two numbers in an array that sum to a target," what is the complexity of the brute-force nested-loop approach?
questions.explanation: Checking every pair with nested loops examines roughly n^2 pairs — the classic brute-force complexity.

questions.prompt: Sorting the array first, then using two pointers moving inward, lands at which complexity for the two-sum problem?
questions.explanation: The two-pointer scan itself is O(n), but the initial sort costs O(n log n), which dominates the overall complexity.

questions.prompt: Using a hash map to record numbers seen so far and checking `target - number` in one pass reaches which complexity?
questions.explanation: A single pass with constant-time hash map lookups gives O(n) — the optimal approach for two-sum.

questions.prompt: Why do interviewers often weight narrating the brute force → better → optimal journey, rather than just seeing the final optimal code?

options.text: Narration is required by law in technical interviews
It demonstrates the ability to reason about trade-offs and complexity incrementally, not just recall a memorized solution
Brute force is always the correct final answer
Narration replaces the need to write any code at all

questions.explanation: Talking through the improvement steps and their complexity shows genuine problem-solving, which can score higher than silently writing optimal code.

questions.prompt: What resource is typically traded for time when moving from an O(n^2) brute-force approach to an O(n) hash-map approach?

options.text: Space (extra memory for the hash map)
Nothing is traded — it's strictly better in every dimension

questions.explanation: The hash map approach uses extra memory to store seen values, trading space for the faster O(n) time complexity.

questions.prompt: For "check if a string has any repeated characters," what data structure typically gets you from a brute-force O(n^2) comparison to an optimal approach?

options.text: A set (or equivalent hash-based structure) to track seen characters
A sorted array with binary search

questions.explanation: Tracking seen characters in a set lets you detect a repeat in a single O(n) pass, replacing the pairwise O(n^2) comparison.

projects.title: 001. Clamp Utility
projects.readmeMarkdown:
# Clamp Utility

## Problem context

API rate limiters and UI sliders need a `clamp` helper that forces a value into `[min, max]` without printing inside the function.

## Goal

Implement `clamp(value, min, max)` with early returns, read three numbers from `stdin`, and print the clamped result.

## Lesson concepts practiced

- [ ] Parameter count and order matter — document what each parameter means.
- [ ] Use early `return` for invalid input instead of deep nesting.
- [ ] Prefer returning values over printing inside helpers.

## Functional requirements

- [ ] Implement `function clamp(value, min, max)` that **returns** a number (no `console.log` inside).
- [ ] If `value < min` → return `min`.
- [ ] If `value > max` → return `max`.
- [ ] Otherwise return `value`.
- [ ] Read `value`, `min`, `max` from `stdin` (one per line).
- [ ] Invalid number → `ERROR: invalid number`.
- [ ] If `min > max` → `ERROR: invalid range`.
- [ ] Print `Result: <clamped>`.

## Non-functional requirements

- [ ] Separate computation (`return`) from I/O (`console.log` / `process.stdout.write`)
- [ ] Use early `return` branches

## Constraints

- [ ] Node.js only
- [ ] `clamp` must be reusable — caller prints the result

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `5`, `0`, `10` → `Result: 5`
- [ ] `-3`, `0`, `10` → `Result: 0`
- [ ] `99`, `0`, `10` → `Result: 10`
- [ ] `5`, `10`, `0` → `ERROR: invalid range`
- [ ] `abc`, `0`, `10` → `ERROR: invalid number`

## Example data

Input:

```
-3
0
10
```

Output:

```
Result: 0
```

## Suggested plan (no solution)

1. Write `clamp` with three early-return paths.
2. Parse stdin numbers in `main`.
3. Call `clamp` and print the labeled result.

## Deliverables

- [ ] Code in `starter/` (`index.js` scaffold + `tests.json` validation cases + `sample.input` example stdin)

## Extensions (optional)

- [ ] Add `clampMany(values, min, max)` returning an array.

quizzes.title: Fundamentals Multiple Choice
quizzes.description: Types, operators, control flow, functions, and truthiness from module 01.

questions.prompt: What is the type of `typeof null` in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: `typeof null` returns `"object"` — a long-standing language quirk. Use `value === null` for null checks.

questions.prompt: What does `"5" + 2` evaluate to?
questions.explanation: The `+` operator coerces the number to a string when one operand is a string, producing concatenation.

questions.prompt: Which keyword declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned?
questions.explanation: `let` is block-scoped and reassignable. `const` is block-scoped but cannot be reassigned. `var` is function-scoped.
`0` is falsy, so the `else` branch runs. Valid data like `0` can still be falsy — do not confuse falsy with invalid.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `null == undefined`?
questions.explanation: Loose equality (`==`) treats `null` and `undefined` as equal. Strict equality (`===`) would be `false`.
The first matching branch wins. `89 >= 90` is false, but `89 >= 80` is true, so `B` prints.
`&&` needs all operands true; `||` needs one true; `!` negates the boolean.

questions.prompt: Which statement about function declarations is correct?

options.text: A function can `return` a value to the caller without printing inside the function
Functions must always use `console.log` to produce output
Parameters are optional and JavaScript ignores extra arguments silently with no effect
A `return` statement is required even when the function returns `undefined`

questions.explanation: Separate computation (`return`) from I/O (`console.log`). Callers decide how to display the returned value.

projects.readmeMarkdown:
# Shallow Merge Guard

## Problem context

Config loaders and reducers often merge a patch object onto a base object — for example, applying user settings on top of defaults. Doing this safely means never mutating the original base object.

## Goal

Implement `shallowMergeGuard(a, b)` that returns a **new** object combining `a` and `b` without mutating either input, read two JSON objects from `stdin`, and print the merged result.

## Lesson concepts practiced

- [ ] Reference vs value — objects are copied by reference, so a "copy" must build a new object rather than reassign the same one.
- [ ] Shallow copy — merge only needs to protect the top-level object; nested values may still be shared references.
- [ ] Guard against invalid input before touching the merge logic.

## Functional requirements

- [ ] Implement `function shallowMergeGuard(a, b)` that **returns** a new object (no `console.log` inside).
- [ ] The result must contain all own enumerable keys of `a`, overwritten by any same-named own enumerable keys of `b`.
- [ ] Any key present only in `b` must be added to the result.
- [ ] The original `a` object must **not** be mutated by the merge.
- [ ] Read two lines from `stdin`: line 1 is JSON object `a`, line 2 is JSON object `b`.
- [ ] If either line fails to parse as JSON → print `ERROR: invalid json`.
- [ ] Otherwise print `JSON.stringify(result)` for the merged object (one line, no `Result:` label).

## Non-functional requirements

- [ ] Separate computation (`shallowMergeGuard`) from I/O (`console.log` / `process.stdout.write`)
- [ ] Use `try`/`catch` around `JSON.parse`, not manual string checks

## Constraints

- [ ] Node.js only
- [ ] Do not mutate the parsed `a` object anywhere in the program
- [ ] Assume both lines, when valid, parse to plain JSON objects (not arrays)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `{"a":1,"b":2}` / `{"b":3,"c":4}` → `{"a":1,"b":3,"c":4}`

# Shallow Merge Guard

## Problem context

Config loaders and reducers often merge a patch object onto a base object — for example, applying user settings on top of defaults. Doing this safely means never mutating the original base object.

## Goal

Implement `shallowMergeGuard(a, b)` that returns a **new** object combining `a` and `b` without mutating either input, read two JSON objects from `stdin`, and print the merged result.

## Lesson concepts practiced

- [ ] Reference vs value — objects are copied by reference, so a "copy" must build a new object rather than reassign the same one.
- [ ] Shallow copy — merge only needs to protect the top-level object; nested values may still be shared references.
- [ ] Guard against invalid input before touching the merge logic.

## Functional requirements

- [ ] Implement `function shallowMergeGuard(a, b)` that **returns** a new object (no `console.log` inside).
- [ ] The result must contain all own enumerable keys of `a`, overwritten by any same-named own enumerable keys of `b`.
- [ ] Any key present only in `b` must be added to the result.
- [ ] The original `a` object must **not** be mutated by the merge.
- [ ] Read two lines from `stdin`: line 1 is JSON object `a`, line 2 is JSON object `b`.
- [ ] If either line fails to parse as JSON → print `ERROR: invalid json`.
- [ ] Otherwise print `JSON.stringify(result)` for the merged object (one line, no `Result:` label).

quizzes.title: Objects, References and Copying Multiple Choice
quizzes.description: Reference vs value, shallow/deep copy, structuredClone, and Object.hasOwn from module 02.

questions.explanation: `b = a` copies the reference, not the object. Both variables point to the same object in memory, so mutating through `b` is visible through `a`.
The spread operator only shallow-copies top-level keys. `copy.profile` still references the same nested object as `original.profile`, so mutating it affects both.

questions.prompt: Which built-in creates a true **deep clone** and preserves types like `Date`, unlike `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value))`?
questions.explanation: `structuredClone` recursively clones nested structures and preserves types such as `Date`, `Map`, and `Set`. `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))` loses `Date` (converts to string) and drops `undefined`/functions. `Object.assign` and spread are only shallow.

questions.prompt: What happens to a `Date` value after `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ when: new Date() }))`?
questions.explanation: `JSON.stringify` serializes `Date` objects via `toISOString()`, producing a string. Parsing that JSON back does not restore the `Date` type — this is a common lossy deep-copy pitfall.

questions.prompt: Given `const user = Object.create({ role: "guest" }); user.name = "Ana";`, what does `Object.hasOwn(user, "role")` return?
questions.explanation: `role` lives on the prototype passed to `Object.create`, not as an own property of `user`. `Object.hasOwn` checks only own enumerable-or-not properties, so it returns `false` even though `"role" in user` would return `true`.
`const` prevents reassigning the `config` binding itself, not mutation of the object it points to. Mutating a property is allowed.
`Array.prototype.sort` mutates the original array in place and returns the same reference, so `nums === sorted` is `true` and `nums` itself is now sorted, starting with `1`.

projects.readmeMarkdown:
# Promise Order Labeler

## Problem context

Debugging async code often starts with predicting *when* each piece of work actually runs — synchronous code first, then queued promise reactions, then timers — rather than the order it was written in.

## Goal

Implement `classifyTokens(tokens)` that groups scheduling tokens by kind, read a line of space-separated tokens from `stdin`, and print them regrouped in the event-loop execution order: sync, then microtasks, then macrotasks.

## Lesson concepts practiced

- [ ] The event loop runs all synchronous code before draining any queue.
- [ ] The microtask queue (promises) fully drains before the next macrotask (timers/callbacks) runs.
- [ ] Within a queue, tasks keep their original relative (FIFO) order.

## Functional requirements

- [ ] Implement `function classifyTokens(tokens)` that **returns** an object with `sync`, `micro`, and `macro` arrays, each preserving the tokens' original encounter order (no `console.log` inside).
- [ ] Read one line from `stdin` containing space-separated tokens, each one of the literal words `sync`, `micro`, or `macro`.
- [ ] If any token is not exactly `sync`, `micro`, or `macro` → print `ERROR: invalid token`.
- [ ] Otherwise print every `sync` token first (one per line, in encounter order), then every `micro` token, then every `macro` token.
- [ ] Each printed token is the literal word (`sync`, `micro`, or `macro`), not an index.

## Non-functional requirements

- [ ] Separate computation (`classifyTokens`) from I/O (`console.log` / `process.stdout.write`)
- [ ] Do not use real `setTimeout`/`Promise` scheduling — this is a conceptual regrouping exercise, not a live event-loop simulation

## Constraints

- [ ] Node.js only
- [ ] Tokens are separated by single spaces on one line; assume no leading/trailing whitespace issues beyond a trailing newline

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `sync micro sync macro` → `sync`, `sync`, `micro`, `macro` (one per line)
- [ ] `sync sync sync` → `sync`, `sync`, `sync`
- [ ] `macro micro sync` → `sync`, `micro`, `macro`
- [ ] `sync macro micro macro sync micro` → `sync`, `sync`, `micro`, `micro`, `macro`, `macro`
- [ ] `sync foo macro` → `ERROR: invalid token`

## Example data

Input:

```
sync micro sync macro
```

Output:

```
sync
sync
micro
macro
```

## Suggested plan (no solution)

1. Read one line from stdin and split it into tokens.
2. Implement `classifyTokens` to bucket each token into `sync`, `micro`, or `macro` arrays, throwing on an unrecognized token.
3. In `main`, catch the thrown error and print `ERROR: invalid token`.
4. Otherwise print `sync` tokens, then `micro` tokens, then `macro` tokens, one per line.

## Deliverables

- [ ] Code in `starter/` (`index.js` scaffold + `tests.json` validation cases + `sample.input` example stdin)

## Extensions (optional)

- [ ] Support a fourth token kind, `microMicro`, that represents a microtask scheduled from inside another microtask, and still prints within the `micro` group.

quizzes.title: Asynchronous JavaScript Multiple Choice
quizzes.description: Event loop, microtasks vs macrotasks, promises, async/await, and error handling from module 03.

questions.explanation: Synchronous code on the call stack always runs first, even before a `setTimeout(0)` callback. The timer callback goes into the task queue and only runs after the current script finishes.
Sync code runs first (`start`, `end`). The event loop then drains the entire microtask queue (promise reactions) before running the next macrotask, so `micro` prints before `macro`.

questions.prompt: What does calling an `async function` always return, even if it has no `await` inside?
questions.explanation: Every `async function` wraps its return value in a `Promise`. Even `async function f() { return 1; }` returns a promise that resolves to `1`, not `1` directly.

questions.prompt: When an `async function` hits an `await`, what happens?

options.text: The entire JavaScript engine blocks until the awaited promise settles
The function pauses and yields control; the rest of the function resumes as a microtask once the promise settles
The function immediately throws if the promise has not settled yet
`await` has no effect unless used inside a `for` loop

questions.explanation: `await` pauses only the current async function; the rest of the program keeps running. When the promise settles, the continuation is scheduled as a microtask, not a blocking operation.

options.text: An unhandled rejection crashes the process

questions.explanation: `try`/`catch` around an `await` catches a rejected promise just like a thrown synchronous error, so the `catch` block runs and prints `caught: boom`.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between `Promise.all` and `Promise.allSettled`?

options.text: `Promise.all` rejects as soon as any input promise rejects; `Promise.allSettled` always resolves with each promise's outcome
`Promise.allSettled` runs promises sequentially; `Promise.all` runs them in parallel
They behave identically but `allSettled` is deprecated
`Promise.all` only accepts a single promise, not an array

questions.explanation: `Promise.all` fails fast: the first rejection short-circuits the whole call. `Promise.allSettled` waits for every promise and reports each as `{ status: "fulfilled", value }` or `{ status: "rejected", reason }`, never rejecting itself.

questions.prompt:
What is printed?

```js
Promise.resolve(1)
  .then((v) => v + 1)
  .then((v) => console.log(v));
console.log("sync");
```
questions.explanation: Both `.then` callbacks are scheduled as microtasks, which only run after the current synchronous code finishes. `console.log("sync")` runs first, then the chained `.then` handlers produce `2`.

quizzes.title: Advanced JavaScript Multiple Choice
quizzes.description: Hoisting/TDZ, closures, higher-order functions, the prototype chain, and ES modules from module 04.

questions.explanation: `var` declarations are hoisted and auto-initialized to `undefined`, so reading `x` before its assignment is legal and prints `"undefined"`.
`let`/`const` are hoisted but stay uninitialized in the Temporal Dead Zone until their declaration line runs — reading early throws.
`count` is captured by reference inside the closure, so each `inc()` call mutates the same private variable that `get()` later reads.
Each call to the factory function creates a fresh, independent closure. Mutating `a`'s private `count` never affects `b`'s.

questions.prompt:
```js
console.log([1, 2, 3].map((n) => n * 2));
```

What is true about the result?

options.text: It is a new array `[2, 4, 6]`; the original array is unchanged
It mutates `[1, 2, 3]` in place and returns the same array
It returns `undefined` because `map` has no return value
It returns a shorter array than the input

questions.explanation: `map` always returns a new array with the same length as the input, one output per input element, and never mutates the original.
`filter` keeps only the elements where the callback returns a truthy value, producing a new (possibly shorter) array — here the two non-empty strings.

options.text: `Object.create` copies `greet` onto `child` as an own property
Calling `child.greet()` throws because `child` has no own `greet`

questions.explanation: `Object.create(proto)` links `child`'s prototype to `parent` without copying properties. `hasOwn` only checks own properties; `in` checks the whole prototype chain.

options.text: `import { default as Widget, default as version } from "./widget.js";`

questions.explanation: A default import has no braces and comes first; named imports use braces. A module can mix one default export with any number of named exports.

# Sliding Window Max Sum

## Problem context

A monitoring dashboard tracks per-minute request counts and needs the busiest contiguous `k`-minute stretch to size autoscaling. Recomputing the sum of every window from scratch is `O(n * k)`; sliding the window and adjusting the running sum by one element at a time is `O(n)`.

## Goal

Read an array of integers and a window size `k` from stdin, then print the maximum sum of any contiguous window of length `k`. If `k` is invalid for the given array, print `ERROR` instead.

## Lesson concepts practiced
- [ ] A sliding window reuses the previous window's sum instead of recomputing it, turning a nested-loop scan into a single pass
- [ ] The window only ever adds the new right-hand element and removes the old left-hand element as it slides — `O(1)` work per step
- [ ] Recognizing when `k` makes the window invalid (`k < 1` or `k > n`) before attempting the slide
- [ ] The sliding window is `O(n)` overall versus `O(n * k)` for recomputing each window's sum independently

## Functional requirements
- [ ] Read line 1: space-separated integers (the array; may contain negative numbers)
- [ ] Read line 2: the integer window size `k`
- [ ] Let `n` be the number of integers read from line 1
- [ ] If `k < 1` or `k > n`, print `ERROR` and stop
- [ ] Otherwise, compute the sum of every contiguous window of exactly `k` elements and print the maximum such sum
- [ ] Use a sliding window (running sum) rather than recomputing each window's sum from scratch
- [ ] Print exactly one line of output ending with a newline

## Non-functional requirements
- [ ] Readability: a single `maxWindowSum(numbers, k)` helper is enough
- [ ] Error handling: invalid `k` prints `ERROR` instead of throwing or printing `NaN`/`undefined`
- [ ] Performance: `O(n)` time — do not recompute the sum of each window with a nested loop

## Constraints
- [ ] Node.js only — no external libraries
- [ ] The array may contain negative numbers, zero, or all-negative values
- [ ] `k` may be `0` or negative, or greater than `n` — both are invalid
- [ ] When `k` equals `n`, the only valid window is the whole array

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Array `2 1 5 1 3 2`, `k = 3` → stdout `9` (window `[5, 1, 3]`)
- [ ] Array `1 2 3`, `k = 5` (k > n) → stdout `ERROR`
- [ ] Array `1 2 3`, `k = 0` (k < 1) → stdout `ERROR`
- [ ] Array `-1 -2 -3 -4`, `k = 2` → stdout `-3` (best of all-negative windows)
- [ ] Array `4 5 6`, `k = 3` (k equals n) → stdout `15` (whole array is the only window)

## Example data

Input:
```text
2 1 5 1 3 2
3
```

Output:
```text
9
```

Input:
```text
1 2 3
5
```

Output:
```text
ERROR
```

## Suggested plan (no solution)
1. Read line 1 into an array of numbers; read line 2 into `k`.
2. If `k < 1` or `k > numbers.length`, print `ERROR` and stop.
3. Compute the sum of the first `k` elements as the initial window sum and track it as the current best.
4. Slide the window one step at a time: add the new element entering on the right, subtract the element leaving on the left, and update the best sum if the new window sum is higher.
5. Print the best sum found after sliding through the whole array.

## Deliverables
- [ ] Code in `starter/` (`index.js` scaffold + `tests.json` validation cases + `sample.input` example stdin)
- [ ] (Optional) reference in `solution/`

## Extensions (optional)
- [ ] Also print the starting index of the best window
- [ ] Support finding the maximum sum for every `k` from `1` to `n` in a single run

- [ ] Array `2 1 5 1 3 2`, `k = 3` → stdout `9` (window `[5, 1, 3]`)
- [ ] Array `1 2 3`, `k = 5` (k > n) → stdout `ERROR`
- [ ] Array `1 2 3`, `k = 0` (k < 1) → stdout `ERROR`
- [ ] Array `-1 -2 -3 -4`, `k = 2` → stdout `-3` (best of all-negative windows)
- [ ] Array `4 5 6`, `k = 3` (k equals n) → stdout `15` (whole array is the only window)

## Example data

Input:
```text

3
```

Output:
```text
9
```

Input:
```text
1 2 3
5
```

Output:
```text
ERROR
```

1. Read line 1 into an array of numbers; read line 2 into `k`.
2. If `k < 1` or `k > numbers.length`, print `ERROR` and stop.
3. Compute the sum of the first `k` elements as the initial window sum and track it as the current best.
4. Slide the window one step at a time: add the new element entering on the right, subtract the element leaving on the left, and update the best sum if the new window sum is higher.
5. Print the best sum found after sliding through the whole array.
