quizzes.title: Node.js and Stdin Check
quizzes.description: Running scripts, stdin, and string input basics.

questions.prompt: How do you run `starter/index.js` with Node.js?
questions.explanation: Node executes `.js` files with the `node` command. This is the standard way to run HackerRank-style solutions locally.

questions.prompt: Input from HackerRank `stdin` arrives as which type?
questions.explanation: Stdin lines are always strings until you parse them explicitly with `Number()` or similar.

questions.prompt: What does `"  Ana  ".trim()` return?
questions.explanation: `trim()` removes leading and trailing whitespace only, leaving the inner text intact.

questions.prompt: Given `const line = "42"`, what is `typeof line`?
questions.explanation: Even numeric-looking input stays a string until converted. `typeof "42"` is `"string"`.

questions.prompt: Why call `rl.close()` after handling input in a one-shot CLI?

options.text: Ends the readline interface and lets the process exit cleanly
Converts stdin strings to numbers automatically

questions.explanation: Without closing the interface, the Node process may keep waiting for more input instead of finishing.

quizzes.title: Output Formatting Check
quizzes.description: Labels, newlines, and readable stdout.

questions.prompt: What does `console.log("Hi")` write to stdout?

options.text: Nothing — it only works in browsers

questions.explanation: `console.log` prints the value and appends `\n`, unlike `process.stdout.write`.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `(12.7).toFixed(2)`?
questions.explanation: `toFixed(2)` returns a string with exactly two digits after the decimal point.

questions.prompt: Which line uses a **template literal**?
questions.explanation: Template literals use backticks and `${...}` interpolation.

questions.prompt: Why label output lines like `Item:` and `Qty:` in challenges?

options.text: Makes results scannable and matches expected test output
Required for Node.js to parse numbers

questions.explanation: Clear labels help humans and automated graders verify each field independently.

questions.prompt: Run: `process.stdout.write("A"); console.log("B");` — what appears on stdout?

options.text: `AB` on one line, then a newline after `B`
`A` on one line, `B` on the next

questions.explanation: `stdout.write` does not add a newline, so `A` and `B` sit on the same line; `console.log` adds `\n` after `B`.

quizzes.title: Comments Check
quizzes.description: Single-line, multi-line comments, and which code actually runs.

questions.explanation: `//` comments out one line; `/* */` comments out a block. Only `A` and `D` run.
The reassignment line is commented out, so `a` stays `1` and `b` is `4`.

questions.prompt: Which syntax starts a **single-line** comment?
questions.explanation: `//` comments the rest of the line. `/* ... */` is for multi-line blocks.

questions.prompt: What happens to code on a line after `//`?

options.text: The engine ignores it — it does not execute
It runs but output is hidden
It runs only in development mode

questions.explanation: Comments are for humans. The JavaScript engine skips them entirely.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer `/* ... */` over `//`?

options.text: When documenting several lines or a short rule list
Whenever a line ends with a semicolon

questions.explanation: Use `/* */` for multi-line notes or blocks; use `//` for one-line explanations.

quizzes.title: let and const Check
quizzes.description: Bindings, reassignment, and const with objects.

questions.explanation: `const` locks the variable binding. Reassigning throws at runtime in strict mode (default in modules).
`const` prevents rebinding the variable, not mutating properties of an object.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer `let` over `const`?

options.text: When the variable will be reassigned later
Whenever the value is a number

questions.explanation: Default to `const`; use `let` when reassignment is intentional (counters, accumulators).

questions.prompt: Given `const original = { n: 1 }; const next = { ...original, n: 2 };` — what is `original.n`?
questions.explanation: Spread creates a new object. `original` is untouched — a safe immutable-style update.

questions.prompt: What does `scores[id] ?? 0` mean when `scores[id]` is missing?

options.text: Use `0` as the default starting score
Throw if the player is unknown

questions.explanation: Nullish coalescing returns the right side when the left is `null` or `undefined` — handy for first-time players.

quizzes.title: Assignment and Reassignment Check
quizzes.description: `=`, compound operators, and `const` rebinding vs mutation.

questions.explanation: `points` becomes `12` via `+=` and `-=`. Mutating `player.score` on a `const` object is allowed.
`const` locks the variable binding. Reassigning the variable itself throws.

questions.prompt: What does `total += 25` mean?
questions.explanation: Compound assignment updates the variable from its current value. `=` assigns; `===` compares.
Changing `limits.max` is fine. Rebinding `limits` to a new object violates `const`.

quizzes.title: Strings Check
quizzes.description: Trim, case, template literals, and normalization.

questions.prompt: What is `"hello".length`?
questions.explanation: `.length` counts characters in the string. `"hello"` has five characters.

questions.prompt: What does `"  a  b  ".trim()` return?
questions.explanation: `trim()` removes only leading/trailing spaces. Internal double space remains.

questions.prompt: How do you compare `"Hello"` and `"HELLO"` case-insensitively?
questions.explanation: Normalize both sides to the same case before strict comparison.

questions.prompt: What does `` `[L${3}] Ana` `` evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Template literals interpolate `${3}` into the string inside backticks.

questions.prompt: Given `const handle = "@AnaS";`, what is `handle.trim().replace(/^@/, "").toLowerCase()`?
questions.explanation: Strip optional `@`, then lowercase — a common handle normalization pipeline.

quizzes.title: Numbers Check
quizzes.description: Parsing stdin, `NaN`, `Number.isFinite`, and `toFixed`.

questions.explanation: `Number("10")` is 15; empty string becomes 0; `abc` is not finite; `toFixed(2)` returns a string.
`10 / 3` is `3.333...`; `toFixed(2)` rounds to two decimal places as a string.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `Number("abc")`?
questions.explanation: Invalid numeric strings become `NaN`. Always validate with `Number.isFinite` before math.

questions.prompt: Which check correctly rejects `NaN` and `Infinity`?
questions.explanation: `Number.isFinite` is false for `NaN`, `Infinity`, and non-numbers. `typeof NaN` is still `"number"`.

questions.prompt: Why trim stdin before `Number(line)`?

options.text: Whitespace around digits can still parse, but empty-after-trim should be validated separately
Trim converts strings to integers only
Trim is required or Node throws

questions.explanation: `Number("  42  ")` works, but `Number("")` is `0` — trim and check emptiness explicitly.

quizzes.title: Booleans Check
quizzes.description: Comparisons, boolean variables, and `Boolean()` conversion.

questions.explanation: 17 is not `>= 18`, but it is a teen (13–19 inclusive).
90 passes, is not perfect, and is in valid range.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `Boolean("")`?
questions.explanation: Empty string is falsy. `Boolean("hello")` would be `true`.

questions.prompt: What does `score >= 60` return when `score` is `85`?
questions.explanation: Comparison operators always produce `true` or `false`.
Whitespace-only input trims to empty string, so `length === 0` is `true`.

quizzes.title: undefined and null Check
quizzes.description: Missing values, strict checks, and labeling behavior.

questions.explanation: Unassigned `let` is `undefined`. `null` is not `undefined`, but `b === null` is `true`.
An empty string is neither `undefined` nor `null` — it is a real value.

questions.prompt: What is `typeof null` in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: `typeof null` is `"object"` for historical reasons. Use `value === null` to test null.

questions.prompt: When should you use `null` instead of `undefined`?

options.text: When your code intentionally means "known to be absent"
Whenever a variable is declared with `let`
Never — they are identical in all cases

questions.explanation: `undefined` is the default "no value yet"; `null` is an explicit empty marker.
Use strict `===` checks. `null` matches the second branch, not the `undefined` branch.

quizzes.title: Arithmetic Operators Check
quizzes.description: Operator precedence, `%`, and string concatenation with `+`.

questions.explanation: `*` before `+`; parentheses override; string `+` concatenates left to right; `%` is remainder.

questions.prompt:
What is printed?

```js
console.log("Total: " + (10 + 5));
```
questions.explanation: Parentheses force numeric addition before concatenation with the string.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `"10" + 5`?
questions.explanation: When one operand is a string, `+` concatenates. Parse with `Number()` before math.

questions.prompt: How do you test whether `n` is even?
questions.explanation: Modulo `%` gives the remainder. Even numbers have remainder 0 when divided by 2.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `10 / 4` in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: JavaScript `/` always produces a float when needed — there is no separate integer division.

quizzes.title: Comparison Operators Check
quizzes.description: Strict vs loose equality, relational operators, and inclusive bounds.

questions.explanation: `===` requires same type and value; `==` coerces; `90 >= 90` is inclusive on the lower bound.
89 is not `>= 90`; strict equality fails against string `"89"`; B-range check passes.

questions.prompt: Which operator should you default to for equality checks?
questions.explanation: Prefer `===` and `!==` to avoid surprise type coercion.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `89 >= 90`?
questions.explanation: 89 is below 90. Off-by-one boundary bugs are common — test edge values like 89 and 90.

questions.prompt: Why parse numeric stdin before comparing with `<` or `>`?

options.text: String comparison uses lexicographic order, not numeric order
stdin is always already a number type

questions.explanation: `"10" < "2"` is `true` as strings. Convert to numbers for numeric comparisons.

quizzes.title: Logical Operators Check
quizzes.description: `&&`, `||`, `!`, and short-circuit evaluation.

questions.explanation: `&&` needs all true; `||` needs one true; `!` negates; both comparisons are true.
105 fails the `<= 100` part of both compound checks.

questions.prompt: When is `canEnter = age >= 18 && hasId` `true`?

options.text: When either age or hasId is true
When age is exactly 18 regardless of hasId

questions.explanation: `&&` requires every part to be true — classic "all checks must pass" validation.

questions.prompt: What does short-circuit mean for `name.length > 0 && name.trim().length > 0` when `name` is `""`?

options.text: The right side is not evaluated because the left is already `false`

questions.explanation: With `&&`, if the left is false, the right is skipped — avoiding errors on empty strings.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `!true`?
questions.explanation: `!` negates a boolean. Prefer positive names like `isValid` over `!isInvalid` when possible.

quizzes.title: if and else Check
quizzes.description: Branching, inclusive boundaries, and early error paths.

questions.explanation: The first matching branch wins. `90 >= 90` is true, so `A` prints.
89 fails the `>= 90` check but passes `>= 80`. Order matters — highest threshold first.

questions.prompt: Why check invalid input in an early `if` branch?

options.text: To print one clear error and avoid falling through to success output
Because `if` only runs once per program
Invalid input automatically throws before `if` runs

questions.explanation: Validate first, then compute the happy path. Do not print both `ERROR:` and a grade.
The condition is false, so the `else` branch runs.
`Number("abc")` is `NaN`, which fails `Number.isFinite` — handle before range checks.

quizzes.title: switch Check
quizzes.description: Case matching, `break`, `default`, and strict equality.

questions.explanation: The `"quit"` case matches and `break` stops fall-through.
Numeric `2` strictly matches `case 2`.

questions.prompt: What happens without `break` after a matching `case`?

options.text: Execution falls through to the next case
The switch restarts from the top

questions.explanation: Missing `break` lets later cases run too — usually a bug unless fall-through is intentional.
`switch` uses strict `===`. String `"1"` does not match number `1`.

questions.prompt: When is `switch` a better fit than `if / else if`?

options.text: When one value maps to fixed constant options (menu commands)

questions.explanation: Use `switch` for discrete constants; use `if / else if` for ranges and complex conditions.

quizzes.title: for Loop Check
quizzes.description: Loop bounds, accumulators, and off-by-one pitfalls.

questions.explanation: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. `<= 4` includes the end value.
2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 20 inclusive.
`i < 3` stops before 3 — classic off-by-one pattern.

questions.prompt: Why initialize `sum = 0` before a summing loop?

options.text: So the accumulator starts from a known value
To make the loop run faster

questions.explanation: Accumulators need a starting point. Uninitialized `sum` would be `undefined` and break math.

options.text: ReferenceError — `i` is block-scoped to the loop

questions.explanation: `let i` in the `for` header is block-scoped — not visible outside the loop.

quizzes.title: while Loop Check
quizzes.description: Sentinel patterns, loop updates, and condition-first iteration.

questions.explanation: When `x` becomes `8`, `x < 8` is false before the next print.

questions.prompt: When does a `while` loop check its condition?

options.text: Once at the end of the program

questions.explanation: If the condition starts false, the body never runs (zero iterations).

questions.prompt: What causes an infinite `while` loop?

options.text: The condition never becomes false because loop variables are not updated

questions.explanation: Every `while` must move toward making the condition false — update variables in the body.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer `while` over `for`?

options.text: When iteration count depends on runtime data (sentinel input)
When you know the exact index range upfront

questions.explanation: Use `for` for known counts; use `while` when stopping depends on data read at runtime.

quizzes.title: Function Declaration Check
quizzes.description: Declaring functions, `return`, and reusable helpers.

questions.explanation: Each call returns the sum of its arguments.

questions.prompt: What does a function without `return` give the caller?
questions.explanation: Functions that only `console.log` inside still return `undefined` unless they `return` a value.

questions.prompt: Why return a value instead of printing inside the helper?

options.text: The caller can reuse the result and decide how to output it
`return` is required for every function or Node exits

questions.explanation: Separate computation from I/O — return values make functions testable and reusable.
`double(5)` returns `10`, stored in `result` and then printed.

quizzes.title: Parameters and Return Values Check
quizzes.description: Arguments, early return, and separating computation from output.

questions.explanation: Each call returns the larger argument via early `return` branches.
5 stays; -3 clamps to min 0; 99 clamps to max 10.
Missing arguments become `undefined`. `2 + undefined` is `NaN` — validate parameters when required.
85 passes; `"x"` is not finite, so early return yields `ERROR`.

questions.prompt: What happens when `return` runs inside a function?

options.text: The function exits immediately — code below does not run
Execution jumps to the next function in the file

questions.explanation: Early `return` is ideal for invalid input — no fall-through to later logic.

quizzes.title: Arrow Functions and Callbacks Check
quizzes.description: Arrow syntax, implicit return, and callbacks with map/filter.

questions.explanation: `map` calls the arrow once per item. Expression-body `(n) => n * 2` returns each doubled value, so the array becomes `[2, 4, 6]`.
A block body `{ ... }` does not auto-return. Without `return`, the caller gets `undefined`. Use `(a, b) => a + b` or `return a + b` inside the block.
`inc` is a callback (a function value). `applyTwice` calls it twice: `5 → 6 → 7`.
`filter` keeps only scores `>= 60`. `map` builds a new array of labels — both use arrow callbacks.
Each element is clamped into `[0, 10]`: `-2 → 0`, `5` stays, `12 → 10`. The callback passed to `map` calls `clamp`.

questions.prompt: Why can you call a `function` declaration before its line in the file, but not a `const` arrow?

options.text: Function declarations are hoisted; `const` arrows are not available before their line

questions.explanation: Declarations are hoisted. An arrow assigned with `const` must be declared before you call it — declare helpers near the top.

quizzes.title: Throwing Errors and Sync try/catch Check
quizzes.description: throw, Error, try/catch/finally, and sync error bubbling.

options.text: `5`, then `caught: Cannot divide by zero`, then `done`
`5`, then `caught: Cannot divide by zero`, then `after divides`, then `done`
Only `caught: Cannot divide by zero` (script crashes before `done`)

questions.explanation: First call prints `5`. The second throws, so `after divides` is skipped; `catch` prints the message, then `done` still runs outside the try.
After `throw`, the rest of the `try` block is skipped. Control jumps to `catch`, which prints `err.message`.

questions.prompt: What does `finally` do in a sync `try` / `catch` / `finally`?

options.text: It always runs — after a successful `try` or after `catch`
It runs only when an error was thrown
It runs only when no error was thrown
It replaces `catch` and receives the error

questions.explanation: `finally` is for cleanup that must happen either way — success or failure.

questions.prompt: A function throws and has no local `try` / `catch`. What happens?

options.text: The error bubbles up to the caller (and further, until caught or the script crashes)
JavaScript converts it to `undefined` and continues
Only that function stops; the caller always keeps running normally
It is silently ignored unless you use `async`

questions.explanation: Sync errors propagate up the call stack. Catch at the level that can handle them; uncaught errors typically crash a Node script.

questions.prompt: Why prefer `throw new Error("Expected a string")` over `throw "Expected a string"`?

options.text: `Error` gives `.message` (and a stack); bare strings make `catch` harder to use consistently
Bare strings cannot be thrown in JavaScript
`new Error` is required for `try` / `catch` to work at all

questions.explanation: You can throw other values, but `Error` is the convention so catch blocks can rely on `err.message` and debugging tools.

quizzes.title: Truthy vs Falsy Check
quizzes.description: Predict boolean conversion in `if` and logical contexts.

questions.prompt: Which value is **falsy** in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: Only `0` is in the falsy set. The string `"0"`, arrays, and objects are all truthy.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `Boolean("0")`?
questions.explanation: Any non-empty string is truthy, including `"0"`. Only the empty string `""` is falsy.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `Boolean([])`?
questions.explanation: Objects (including arrays) are always truthy, even when empty. Check `arr.length === 0` instead of `if (arr)`.

questions.prompt: A form field returns numeric `0`. Which check treats `0` as **missing** by mistake?
questions.explanation: `0` is falsy, so `if (!value)` treats it as missing. Use nullish checks or explicit validation when `0` is valid.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `Boolean(" ")` (a string with one space)?
questions.explanation: Only the empty string `""` is falsy. A string with whitespace is still non-empty and therefore truthy.

quizzes.title: Equality and Coercion Check
quizzes.description: Predict `==` vs `===` and common coercion traps.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `"0" === 0`?
questions.explanation: Strict equality compares type and value. A string is never strictly equal to a number.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `"0" == 0`?
questions.explanation: Loose equality coerces the string to a number before comparing, so `"0"` and `0` match.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `[] == 0`?
questions.explanation: `[]` coerces to `""`, then to `0` in numeric comparison. This is why `==` surprises people — prefer `===`.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `{} == {}`?
questions.explanation: Objects are compared by reference, not by structure. Two object literals are different references.

questions.prompt: Which comparison is **`true`**?
questions.explanation: `[1]` coerces to `"1"` then `1` under `==`. Strict equality does not coerce types, so `[1] === 1` is false.

quizzes.title: Type Coercion Check
quizzes.description: Predict loose equality (`==`) outcomes.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `"" == 0`?
questions.explanation: Empty string coerces to `0` in numeric loose equality.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `false == 0`?
questions.explanation: Boolean `false` coerces to `0` when compared with `==` to a number.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `[] == false`?
questions.explanation: `[]` coerces through `''` and `0`, matching `false` under loose equality.

questions.prompt: Which expression is **`false`**?
questions.explanation: `null` only loosely equals `undefined` — not `0` or other values.

questions.prompt: Best default for comparisons in application code?

options.text: Use `===` unless you have a documented reason for `==`
Always use `==` — it is more flexible

questions.explanation: Strict equality avoids accidental coercion. Convert types explicitly when needed.

quizzes.title: typeof and Array.isArray Check
quizzes.description: Predict typeof tags and when Array.isArray is required.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `typeof null`?
questions.explanation: Legacy quirk: `typeof null` is `"object"`. Never use `typeof` to detect null — compare with `=== null`.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `typeof []`?
questions.explanation: Arrays are objects under `typeof`. Use `Array.isArray` to detect arrays.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `Array.isArray({ length: 2 })`?
questions.explanation: Array-like objects are not arrays. `Array.isArray` returns `true` only for real arrays.

questions.prompt: Which check correctly reports an array (not a plain object)?
questions.explanation: `typeof` never returns `"array"`, and `"object"` also matches plain objects and `null`. Prefer `Array.isArray`.

questions.prompt: In a safe `describe(value)` helper, what order should you check?
questions.explanation: Check `null` first (because `typeof null === "object"`), then arrays, then fall back to `typeof`.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `typeof Number`?
questions.explanation: `Number` is a built-in function (constructor). Functions get the special tag `"function"`.

quizzes.title: Nullish Operators Check
quizzes.description: `null`, `undefined`, `== null`, `?.`, and `??`.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `null == undefined`?
questions.explanation: Loose equality has a special rule: `null` and `undefined` are equal to each other (and only each other).

questions.prompt: What is the result of `null === undefined`?
questions.explanation: Strict equality requires the same type. `null` and `undefined` are different types.

questions.prompt: Given `const x = 0`, what is `x ?? 10`?
questions.explanation: Nullish coalescing (`??`) only replaces `null` or `undefined`. `0` is kept because it is not nullish.

questions.prompt: Given `const x = 0`, what is `x || 10`?
questions.explanation: `||` uses truthiness. `0` is falsy, so the right-hand side `10` is returned.

questions.prompt: What does `user?.address?.zip` return when `user` is `null`?
questions.explanation: Optional chaining short-circuits on `null`/`undefined` and yields `undefined` instead of throwing.

quizzes.title: Array Literals Indexing and length Check
quizzes.description: Predict indexes, missing slots, and how .length changes.

questions.prompt: Given `const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];` what is `fruits[0]`?
questions.explanation: Array indexes start at `0`. The first element is `fruits[0]` → `"apple"`.

questions.prompt: Given `const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];` what is `fruits[3]`?
questions.explanation: A missing index returns `undefined` — it does not throw.

questions.prompt: Given `const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];` what is `fruits.length`?
questions.explanation: `.length` is the number of elements the array reports. Three items → `3`.

questions.prompt: How do you read the **last** element of a non-empty array `arr`?
questions.explanation: Valid indexes run `0` … `length - 1`. `arr[arr.length]` is out of range and yields `undefined`.

questions.prompt: After `const xs = [1, 2, 3]; xs[3] = 4;` what is `xs.length`?
questions.explanation: Writing past the end extends the array. `xs[3] = 4` appends one item and grows `.length` to `4`.

questions.prompt: After `const letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d"]; letters.length = 2;` what is `letters[2]`?
questions.explanation: Shortening `.length` truncates the array. Indexes `2` and beyond are gone → `undefined`.

quizzes.title: Fundamentals Check
quizzes.description: Truthy/falsy, equality, and basic operators.

questions.prompt: Which values are **falsy** in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: The classic falsy set is: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, and NaN. The string '0' is truthy.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `null == undefined`?
questions.explanation: Loose equality treats null and undefined as equal. Strict equality (`===`) would be false.

questions.prompt: What does `typeof null` return?
questions.explanation: This is a long-standing JavaScript quirk: typeof null is 'object'. Prefer `value === null` for null checks.

questions.prompt: Which expression coerces a value to boolean without changing the original?
questions.explanation: Double negation (`!!`) converts to boolean. The other options change type or value.

quizzes.title: Fundamentals Multiple Choice
quizzes.description: Types, operators, control flow, functions, and truthiness from module 01.

questions.prompt: What is the type of `typeof null` in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: `typeof null` returns `"object"` — a long-standing language quirk. Use `value === null` for null checks.

questions.prompt: What does `"5" + 2` evaluate to?
questions.explanation: The `+` operator coerces the number to a string when one operand is a string, producing concatenation.

questions.prompt: Which keyword declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned?
questions.explanation: `let` is block-scoped and reassignable. `const` is block-scoped but cannot be reassigned. `var` is function-scoped.
`0` is falsy, so the `else` branch runs. Valid data like `0` can still be falsy — do not confuse falsy with invalid.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `null == undefined`?
questions.explanation: Loose equality (`==`) treats `null` and `undefined` as equal. Strict equality (`===`) would be `false`.
The first matching branch wins. `89 >= 90` is false, but `89 >= 80` is true, so `B` prints.
`&&` needs all operands true; `||` needs one true; `!` negates the boolean.

questions.prompt: Which statement about function declarations is correct?

options.text: A function can `return` a value to the caller without printing inside the function
Functions must always use `console.log` to produce output
Parameters are optional and JavaScript ignores extra arguments silently with no effect
A `return` statement is required even when the function returns `undefined`

questions.explanation: Separate computation (`return`) from I/O (`console.log`). Callers decide how to display the returned value.

quizzes.title: Object Literals and Property Access Check
quizzes.description: Create objects and read/update properties with dot and bracket notation.

questions.explanation: `age` was updated to 37. Missing keys like `city` return `undefined`, not an error.

questions.prompt: Given `const key = "name"` and `const user = { name: "Ada" }`, what is the difference between `user.key` and `user[key]`?
questions.explanation: Dot notation looks for a property literally named `key`. Bracket notation uses the value of the variable (`"name"`).

questions.prompt: When is bracket notation **required** (dot notation cannot work)?

options.text: When the key comes from a variable or is not a valid identifier

questions.explanation: Dot needs a fixed identifier. Dynamic keys and keys with spaces/punctuation need brackets.

questions.prompt: Does `const user = { name: "Ada" }` prevent mutating `user.name`?

options.text: No — `const` only blocks reassigning the variable `user`
Yes — property writes throw in all modes
Only if the property was created with `let`

questions.explanation: `const` freezes the binding, not the object. You can still update properties unless you use `Object.freeze`.

questions.prompt: What does reading a missing property return?
questions.explanation: Missing own keys evaluate to `undefined`; they do not throw.

quizzes.title: Computed Keys and Shorthand Check
quizzes.description: Property shorthand and computed keys in object literals.

questions.explanation: Shorthand `{ name }` means `{ name: name }`. `[field]` evaluates to the string `"role"`.

questions.prompt: What does `{ name, age }` mean when `name` and `age` are variables?

options.text: Same as `{ name: name, age: age }`
Creates keys from the string values of the variables

questions.explanation: Property shorthand reuses the variable name as both key and value.

questions.prompt: Given `const key = "name"`, which literal creates a property named `"name"`?
questions.explanation: `{ key: "Ada" }` always creates a property literally named `key`. Computed keys use `[key]`.

questions.prompt: When are computed keys evaluated?

options.text: Only when the property is first read

questions.explanation: The expression inside `[...]` runs when the literal is evaluated, and the resulting string/symbol becomes the key.

questions.prompt: What is `{ [`${prefix}Id`]: id }` with `prefix = "user"` and `id = 7`?
questions.explanation: Template literals inside computed keys are evaluated, so the key becomes `userId`.

quizzes.title: Object Destructuring Check
quizzes.description: Unpack object fields with defaults, renaming, and nesting.

questions.explanation: `name` and `city` unpack from the object. Missing `role` gets the default `"guest"`.

questions.prompt: What does `const { name: fullName } = user` do?
questions.explanation: Destructuring rename uses `source: localName`. The object itself is unchanged.

questions.prompt: When does a destructuring default apply?

options.text: When the value is `undefined` (missing key or explicit undefined)

questions.explanation: Defaults trigger only for `undefined`. `null`, `0`, and `""` are kept as-is.

questions.prompt: What happens with `const { name } = null`?
questions.explanation: Destructuring requires an object-like target. Guard with `user ?? {}` when input may be nullish.

questions.prompt: How do you unpack nested `pages` from `{ title: "Report", meta: { pages: 3 } }`?
questions.explanation: Nest the pattern: `meta: { pages }` mirrors the object shape.

quizzes.title: Rest and Spread Check
quizzes.description: Shallow copy, override, and rest leftovers for objects and arrays.

questions.explanation: Rest gathers leftover keys. Spread copies then `b: 99` overrides — later keys win.

questions.prompt: What is true about object spread `{ ...state }` when `state` has nested objects?

options.text: Top-level is new; nested objects are still shared references

questions.explanation: Spread is shallow. Mutating `next.user.name` still changes `state.user.name`.

questions.prompt: In `{ ...a, ...b }`, which source wins on conflicting keys?
questions.explanation: Properties are copied left to right; later keys overwrite earlier ones.

questions.prompt: Where must object rest (`...rest`) appear in a destructuring pattern?
questions.explanation: Rest must be last so it can collect whatever was not already bound.

questions.prompt: How do you drop `id` from `{ id: 10, name: "Ada", active: true }` without listing every other key?
questions.explanation: Pull `id` out (even if unused) and rest collects the remaining own enumerable keys into a new object.

quizzes.title: Object.keys values and entries Check
quizzes.description: Turn objects into key/value/entry lists for iteration.

questions.explanation: `keys` → names, `values` → values, `entries` → `[key, value]` pairs.

questions.prompt: Which keys do `Object.keys` / `values` / `entries` include?
questions.explanation: These methods skip the prototype chain and non-enumerable / Symbol keys (for the usual string-key case).

questions.prompt: Given a prototype property `inherited` and own `own`, what does `Object.keys(obj)` return?
questions.explanation: `in` would see inherited keys; `Object.keys` does not.

questions.prompt: Does mutating the array returned by `Object.keys(obj)` change `obj`?

options.text: No — you get a new array

questions.explanation: The result is a fresh array. Changing it does not rename or remove object properties.

questions.prompt: Which loop pattern pairs naturally with `Object.entries`?

options.text: `for (const key of Object.entries(obj))` where key is a string

questions.explanation: Each entry is a two-element array, so destructuring `[key, value]` is the usual form.

quizzes.title: Object.fromEntries Check
quizzes.description: Rebuild objects from [key, value] pairs after map/filter.

questions.explanation: `fromEntries` builds an object from an iterable of `[key, value]` pairs.

questions.prompt: What is the inverse of `Object.entries`?
questions.explanation: `entries` → pairs; `fromEntries` → object. Together they enable map/filter/rebuild.

questions.prompt: If pairs contain duplicate keys, what happens?

options.text: Values are merged into an array

questions.explanation: `Object.fromEntries([["a",1],["a",2]])` yields `{ a: 2 }` with no error.

questions.prompt: How do you remove `password` from a plain object using entries?
questions.explanation: Filter the pairs, then rebuild with `fromEntries`. `filter` on entries returns an array, not an object.

questions.prompt: Can `Object.fromEntries` accept a `Map`?

options.text: Yes — Maps are iterables of `[key, value]` pairs
Only if the Map keys are numbers

questions.explanation: Any iterable of pairs works, including `Map`.

quizzes.title: Object.assign and Merging Check
quizzes.description: Shallow merge with Object.assign and object spread.

questions.explanation: Target `{}` receives copies. Later `prefs` overwrites `lang`. `defaults` is not the target, so it stays intact.

questions.prompt: What is the modern literal equivalent of `Object.assign({}, a, b)`?
questions.explanation: Object spread performs the same shallow merge into a new object.

questions.prompt: What does `Object.assign(target, { b: 2 })` do to `target`?

options.text: Mutates `target` by copying properties onto it
Always returns a brand-new object and leaves `target` alone

questions.explanation: The first argument is the mutable target. Pass `{}` when you want a new object.

questions.prompt: Is `Object.assign` / `{ ... }` a deep merge for nested objects?

options.text: No — nested objects are replaced wholesale (shallow)
Yes — nested keys are merged recursively
Only when both sides have the same keys

questions.explanation: `{ nested: { a: 1 } }` merged with `{ nested: { b: 2 } }` yields `{ nested: { b: 2 } }`, not `{ a: 1, b: 2 }`.

questions.prompt: In `Object.assign({}, { x: 1 }, { x: 2 }, { x: 3 })`, what is `x`?
questions.explanation: Sources are applied left to right; the last write to `x` remains.

quizzes.title: Reference vs Value Check
quizzes.description: Predict when variables share objects vs copy primitives.

questions.explanation: Primitives copy by value. Reassigning `b` does not change `a`.
`b = a` creates an alias. Mutating through `b` changes the same object that `a` references.
`b = { n: 999 }` is reassignment (new object), not mutation. `a.n = 2` mutates the original object only.

questions.prompt: Which assignment creates an **alias** (two variables referencing the same object)?

options.text: `const b = a` when `a` is an object
`let b = a` when `a` is a number
`let b = a + 1` when `a` is a number

questions.explanation: Assigning an object variable to another creates a reference alias. Spread creates a new top-level object (shallow copy), and primitives copy by value.

questions.prompt: Which of these is **mutation** (changing an existing value in place)?

options.text: `let b = a` when `a` is a number

questions.explanation: Setting a property on an existing object mutates it. Reassignment and spread create new bindings or containers.

quizzes.title: Shallow Copy Check
quizzes.description: Predict nested sharing with spread and copy-on-write patterns.

questions.explanation: Object spread is shallow: `copy` is new, but `copy.address` and `user.address` still point to the same nested object.
Array spread is also shallow. The outer array is new, but elements inside are still shared references.

questions.prompt:
Which update **does not** mutate the original `user`?

```js
const user = { name: "Ana", address: { city: "SP" } };
```
questions.explanation: Copy-on-write replaces every nested level you change. Options b–d mutate shared nested data or the original object.

questions.prompt: What is true about `{ ...obj }` and `Object.assign({}, obj)`?

options.text: Both create a shallow copy of the top level only
Both create a deep copy of all nested objects
Spread is deep; Object.assign is shallow
Neither copies anything; both create aliases

questions.explanation: Spread and Object.assign copy enumerable own properties into a new object. Nested values are still shared references.

questions.prompt: Given `const state = { items: [{ id: 1, qty: 1 }] };`, which pattern correctly increments `qty` without mutating `state`?

options.text: Build `nextState` with spread at both the `items` array and the changed item object

questions.explanation: Shallow copy of `state` or `items` still shares inner item objects. You must copy the array and replace the changed item.

quizzes.title: Deep Copy Check
quizzes.description: JSON clone limits vs structuredClone for snapshots.

questions.explanation: JSON serialization turns `Date` into an ISO string. JSON cloning is lossy for many types.
`JSON.stringify` throws on `BigInt`. That is another reason JSON cloning is not a universal deep-copy solution.

questions.prompt: What happens to `undefined` values in nested objects when using `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))`?
questions.explanation: JSON cannot represent `undefined`. During serialization, object properties with `undefined` values are omitted.

questions.prompt: After `const y = structuredClone(x)` where `x = { when: new Date(), set: new Set([1, 2]) }`, which is true?
questions.explanation: `structuredClone` preserves supported built-in types like `Date` and `Set`, unlike JSON cloning.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer a deep copy over shallow copy + copy-on-write?

options.text: When you need an immutable snapshot boundary and cannot risk shared nested references
For every variable assignment in the program
Never — deep copy is always wrong

questions.explanation: Deep copies are expensive. Use them when you truly need isolation; otherwise prefer targeted copy-on-write updates.

quizzes.title: Object.hasOwn Check
quizzes.description: Own properties vs inherited prototype chain.

questions.explanation: `shared` is on the prototype, not an own property. `"shared" in user` is true, but `Object.hasOwn` returns false for inherited keys.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `"key" in obj` and `Object.hasOwn(obj, "key")`?

options.text: `in` includes inherited keys; `hasOwn` checks only own properties

questions.explanation: The `in` operator walks the prototype chain. `Object.hasOwn` asks whether the property exists directly on the object.

questions.prompt: For a plain object `record = { id: 1 }`, what is `Object.hasOwn(record, "toString")`?
questions.explanation: `toString` is inherited from `Object.prototype`, not an own property of `record`.

questions.prompt: Why prefer `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` over `obj.hasOwnProperty(key)` in library code?

options.text: Some objects may null out or override `hasOwnProperty`
`Object.hasOwn` is slower but required by syntax

questions.explanation: `Object.hasOwn` is the safe built-in that does not rely on the object possibly missing or overriding `hasOwnProperty`.
Assigning `config.theme = "light"` creates an own property shadowing the prototype. Reading `config.theme` returns `"light"`.

quizzes.title: References & Copying Check
quizzes.description: Reference vs value, shallow copy pitfalls, and deep copy.

questions.explanation: Primitives copy by value. Reassigning `b` does not change `a`.
`b = a` creates an alias. Mutating through `b` changes the same object that `a` references.
Object spread is shallow: `copy` is new, but `copy.address` and `user.address` still point to the same nested object.
Array spread is also shallow. The outer array is new, but elements inside are still shared references.
`b = { n: 999 }` is reassignment (new object), not mutation. `a.n = 2` mutates the original object only.
JSON serialization turns `Date` into an ISO string. JSON cloning is lossy for many types.
`JSON.stringify` throws on `BigInt`. That is another reason JSON cloning is not a universal deep-copy solution.

quizzes.title: Objects, References and Copying Multiple Choice
quizzes.description: Reference vs value, shallow/deep copy, structuredClone, and Object.hasOwn from module 02.

questions.explanation: `b = a` copies the reference, not the object. Both variables point to the same object in memory, so mutating through `b` is visible through `a`.
The spread operator only shallow-copies top-level keys. `copy.profile` still references the same nested object as `original.profile`, so mutating it affects both.

questions.prompt: Which built-in creates a true **deep clone** and preserves types like `Date`, unlike `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value))`?
questions.explanation: `structuredClone` recursively clones nested structures and preserves types such as `Date`, `Map`, and `Set`. `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))` loses `Date` (converts to string) and drops `undefined`/functions. `Object.assign` and spread are only shallow.

questions.prompt: What happens to a `Date` value after `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ when: new Date() }))`?
questions.explanation: `JSON.stringify` serializes `Date` objects via `toISOString()`, producing a string. Parsing that JSON back does not restore the `Date` type — this is a common lossy deep-copy pitfall.

questions.prompt: Given `const user = Object.create({ role: "guest" }); user.name = "Ana";`, what does `Object.hasOwn(user, "role")` return?
questions.explanation: `role` lives on the prototype passed to `Object.create`, not as an own property of `user`. `Object.hasOwn` checks only own enumerable-or-not properties, so it returns `false` even though `"role" in user` would return `true`.
`const` prevents reassigning the `config` binding itself, not mutation of the object it points to. Mutating a property is allowed.
`Array.prototype.sort` mutates the original array in place and returns the same reference, so `nums === sorted` is `true` and `nums` itself is now sorted, starting with `1`.

quizzes.title: Single-Threaded Execution Check
quizzes.description: Predict sync vs scheduled setTimeout order on one thread.

questions.explanation: Synchronous logs run to completion first (`A`, then `C`). `setTimeout` only schedules `B` for later, even with delay `0`.

questions.prompt: What does `setTimeout(fn, 0)` do on the current synchronous pass?

options.text: Runs `fn` immediately before the next line
Pauses the thread for 0 ms then runs `fn`
Schedules `fn` for later; sync code keeps running
Cancels all other timers and runs `fn`

questions.explanation: `setTimeout` schedules a callback. It does not pause the current line or jump ahead of remaining sync work.

options.text: Because `4` is scheduled as a microtask
Because sync code finishes before any timer callback runs
Because nested timers run before outer timers
Because `console.log(4)` has higher priority than timers

questions.explanation: `1` and `4` are synchronous. The outer timer callback (which prints `2`) cannot run until the call stack is clear of that sync pass.

questions.prompt: When is the inner `setTimeout` that prints `3` scheduled in the nested example?

options.text: At the same time as the outer timer is registered
Only after the outer timer callback starts running

questions.explanation: The inner timer is registered inside the outer callback, so it cannot be scheduled until that callback runs after sync work finishes.

quizzes.title: Call Stack Check
quizzes.description: Trace push/pop of stack frames for synchronous calls.

questions.explanation: `first` waits while `second` runs on top of the stack. `after second` prints only after `second` returns.

questions.prompt: At the exact moment `"second"` prints in the first example, which frame is on top of the call stack?
questions.explanation: `second` is the currently executing frame. `first` is waiting underneath until `second` returns.

questions.prompt: What happens when a function recursively calls itself with no exit condition?

options.text: The event loop skips it and continues
It becomes a microtask and waits
The call stack grows until `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`
Node automatically moves it to a worker thread

questions.explanation: Infinite recursion keeps pushing frames until the engine throws a maximum call stack size error.

questions.prompt: Why can a `setTimeout` callback **not** jump onto the call stack while `first()` is still running?

options.text: Timers are ignored until the process exits
Current synchronous frames must finish (pop) before the event loop runs queued callbacks
Because Promise microtasks always cancel timers

questions.explanation: Scheduled callbacks wait until the current synchronous stack is clear. The event loop cannot interleave them mid-call-chain.

quizzes.title: Event Loop Check
quizzes.description: Order sync, microtasks, and tasks with the event loop model.

questions.explanation: Sync first (`start`, `end`), then drain microtasks (`micro`), then run the timer task (`timer`).

questions.prompt: In the event-loop mental model, what happens immediately after synchronous code empties the call stack?

options.text: Run one timer task, then drain microtasks
Block until the next network packet arrives

questions.explanation: After sync work, the engine drains microtasks completely before taking the next task from the task queue.

questions.prompt: How should you classify `Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("B"))`?
questions.explanation: Promise reactions (`.then` callbacks) are microtasks, not timer tasks.
`A` and `D` are sync. `B` is a microtask and runs before the `setTimeout` task `C`.

quizzes.title: Callback and Microtask Queues Check
quizzes.description: Compare Promise microtasks vs setTimeout tasks.

questions.explanation: After sync (`start`, `end`), the microtask queue drains before the next timer task.

questions.prompt:
For chained microtasks:

```js
Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => console.log("m1"))
  .then(() => console.log("m2"));
setTimeout(() => console.log("t1"), 0);
```

What is the order?
questions.explanation: The microtask queue is drained completely — so both `m1` and `m2` run before task `t1`.

questions.prompt: What does `setTimeout(fn, 0)` mean in practice?

options.text: Schedule `fn` as a task after current sync work and after microtasks drain
Run `fn` on a background thread for 0 ms

questions.explanation: Delay `0` still queues a macrotask. It runs after the current sync pass and after the microtask queue is empty.

questions.prompt: Promise `.then` callbacks are queued as:

options.text: Idle callbacks with lower priority than timers

questions.explanation: Promise reactions are microtasks. That is why they usually run before `setTimeout(..., 0)` callbacks.

quizzes.title: Promises Check
quizzes.description: Predict Promise settlement and .then/.catch timing.

questions.explanation: `.then` reactions run as microtasks after the current synchronous code. `after` prints first.

questions.prompt: Which Promise states are valid?

options.text: resolved only — rejected is not a state

questions.explanation: A Promise is pending until it becomes fulfilled or rejected.

questions.prompt: How do you typically handle a rejected Promise in a chain?

options.text: Rejections cannot be handled in JavaScript

questions.explanation: `.catch` handles rejections in the Promise chain (and rejection handlers in `.then` can too).

questions.prompt: In `new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... })`, when do `.then` callbacks run?

options.text: Synchronously inside the executor, before it returns
Later as microtasks after the Promise settles

questions.explanation: `resolve`/`reject` settle the Promise; `.then` reactions are scheduled as microtasks afterward.

quizzes.title: Async/Await Check
quizzes.description: Predict await resume order and try/catch around await.

questions.explanation: `main()` runs synchronously until `await`, printing `A`. Then `C` runs. `B` resumes later as a microtask.

questions.prompt: What does an `async` function always return?
questions.explanation: An `async` function always returns a Promise, even if you `return` a plain value.

questions.prompt: How does `await` on a rejected Promise behave inside an `async` function?

options.text: It converts the rejection into a timer task

questions.explanation: `await` on a rejection throws inside the async function. Catch it with `try/catch` (or handle the returned Promise).

questions.prompt: Code after `await` resumes as:

options.text: Immediate sync work ahead of `console.log` in the caller

questions.explanation: `await` pauses the async function and schedules the continuation as a microtask after the awaited Promise settles.

quizzes.title: Try/Catch Async Errors Check
quizzes.description: Handle Promise rejections with try/catch and toResult.

questions.explanation: `await` on a rejection throws inside the async function, so `try/catch` logs `caught boom`.

questions.prompt: If an `async` function throws (or rejects), what happens to its returned Promise?
questions.explanation: Throwing or rejecting inside `async` rejects the Promise that the function returned.

questions.prompt: What does a successful `toResult(promise)` typically return?
questions.explanation: The `toResult` pattern normalizes success into `{ ok: true, value }` so callers can branch without `try/catch`.

questions.prompt: Why use `toResult` instead of only relying on uncaught rejections?

options.text: It makes Promises run on multiple threads
Callers can branch on `{ ok, value }` vs `{ ok: false, error }` without crashing
It converts sync errors into `setTimeout` callbacks

questions.explanation: `toResult` turns fulfillment/rejection into a plain result object so callers can handle both paths explicitly.

quizzes.title: Async & Event Loop Check
quizzes.description: Sync vs async, microtasks, promises, and async/await.

questions.prompt: Which queue runs **before** the next macrotask after the call stack is empty?
questions.explanation: After synchronous code, the engine drains the microtask queue completely before taking the next macrotask.

questions.prompt: What does `await` do inside an async function?

options.text: Pauses that function and resumes when the promise settles
Blocks the entire JavaScript thread globally
Always runs the awaited code on a worker thread

questions.explanation: await suspends the async function, not the whole runtime. Other tasks can still run via the event loop.

questions.prompt: A rejected promise without `.catch()` or try/catch around await becomes…

options.text: An unhandled rejection (and should be handled in production code)

questions.explanation: Unhandled rejections are a common production bug. Always handle errors on async boundaries.

questions.prompt: `setTimeout(fn, 0)` schedules `fn` as a…
questions.explanation: Even with 0ms delay, setTimeout callbacks are macrotasks and run after microtasks.

quizzes.title: Asynchronous JavaScript Multiple Choice
quizzes.description: Event loop, microtasks vs macrotasks, promises, async/await, and error handling from module 03.

questions.explanation: Synchronous code on the call stack always runs first, even before a `setTimeout(0)` callback. The timer callback goes into the task queue and only runs after the current script finishes.
Sync code runs first (`start`, `end`). The event loop then drains the entire microtask queue (promise reactions) before running the next macrotask, so `micro` prints before `macro`.

questions.prompt: What does calling an `async function` always return, even if it has no `await` inside?
questions.explanation: Every `async function` wraps its return value in a `Promise`. Even `async function f() { return 1; }` returns a promise that resolves to `1`, not `1` directly.

questions.prompt: When an `async function` hits an `await`, what happens?

options.text: The entire JavaScript engine blocks until the awaited promise settles
The function pauses and yields control; the rest of the function resumes as a microtask once the promise settles
The function immediately throws if the promise has not settled yet
`await` has no effect unless used inside a `for` loop

questions.explanation: `await` pauses only the current async function; the rest of the program keeps running. When the promise settles, the continuation is scheduled as a microtask, not a blocking operation.

options.text: An unhandled rejection crashes the process

questions.explanation: `try`/`catch` around an `await` catches a rejected promise just like a thrown synchronous error, so the `catch` block runs and prints `caught: boom`.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between `Promise.all` and `Promise.allSettled`?

options.text: `Promise.all` rejects as soon as any input promise rejects; `Promise.allSettled` always resolves with each promise's outcome
`Promise.allSettled` runs promises sequentially; `Promise.all` runs them in parallel
They behave identically but `allSettled` is deprecated
`Promise.all` only accepts a single promise, not an array

questions.explanation: `Promise.all` fails fast: the first rejection short-circuits the whole call. `Promise.allSettled` waits for every promise and reports each as `{ status: "fulfilled", value }` or `{ status: "rejected", reason }`, never rejecting itself.

questions.prompt:
What is printed?

```js
Promise.resolve(1)
  .then((v) => v + 1)
  .then((v) => console.log(v));
console.log("sync");
```
questions.explanation: Both `.then` callbacks are scheduled as microtasks, which only run after the current synchronous code finishes. `console.log("sync")` runs first, then the chained `.then` handlers produce `2`.

quizzes.title: Hoisting and TDZ Check
quizzes.description: Predict what var, let, and const do when read before their declaration line.

questions.explanation: `var x` is hoisted and auto-initialized to `undefined` before the assignment line runs.
`let` is hoisted but stays in the Temporal Dead Zone until its declaration runs — reading it early throws a `ReferenceError`.
`const` follows the same TDZ rule as `let` — hoisted but uninitialized until the declaration line.

questions.prompt: After execution passes a `let` declaration's line, how does the binding behave?

options.text: Behaves like a normal, initialized variable

questions.explanation: The TDZ ends exactly at the declaration line — after that, `let`/`const` behave like any other variable.

questions.prompt: Where does the Temporal Dead Zone end for a given `let`/`const` binding?

options.text: At the end of the enclosing block
At the end of the file

questions.explanation: The TDZ starts at the top of the scope and ends exactly when the declaration line executes — not at the block's closing brace.

questions.prompt: Which statement about hoisting is true?

options.text: Only `var` is hoisted; `let`/`const` are not hoisted at all
`var`, `let`, and `const` are all hoisted, but only `var` is auto-initialized to `undefined`
Hoisting only applies inside functions, never at module scope

questions.explanation: All three are hoisted (the engine reserves the binding), but `var` is immediately set to `undefined` while `let`/`const` stay uninitialized (TDZ) until their line runs.

quizzes.title: Closures Check
quizzes.description: Predict how closures capture and mutate private state across factory calls.

questions.prompt: What is a closure?

options.text: A function bundled with references to variables from its creation scope
A copy of all global variables made at function definition time
A special syntax for defining classes
A way to prevent a function from being called twice

questions.explanation: A closure is a function paired with references to the variables from the scope where it was created, even after that scope has returned.
`count` starts at 5 and each `inc()` call mutates the same closed-over variable, ending at 7.
Each call to the factory function creates a fresh, independent closure. Mutating `a`'s `count` never affects `b`'s `count`.

questions.prompt: Why can't outside code read `count` directly in the counter example?

options.text: Because `count` is declared with `let` inside the factory and never exposed on the returned object
Because JavaScript objects cannot have numeric properties
It actually can be read directly; closures don't provide privacy

questions.explanation: `count` only exists inside the factory's scope. The only access paths are the methods (`inc`, `dec`, `get`) that the factory chooses to return.

questions.prompt: Does a closure capture a snapshot (value) or a live reference to its outer variable?

options.text: A snapshot taken at the moment the closure is created
A live reference — later mutations to the variable are visible inside the closure
Neither — closures cannot access outer variables at all
It depends on whether the variable is a primitive or an object

questions.explanation: Closures capture variables by reference. If the outer variable changes after the closure is created, the closure sees the updated value.
First call flips `on` from `false` to `true` (returns `true`, discarded). Second call flips it back to `false` and returns `false`.

quizzes.title: Higher-Order Functions Check
quizzes.description: Predict the output length and content of map/filter pipelines.

questions.prompt: What is a higher-order function?

options.text: A function that takes a function as an argument, returns a function, or both
Any function declared with `function` instead of an arrow
A function that always returns a number
A function that cannot be reassigned

questions.explanation: Higher-order functions operate on other functions — by accepting them as arguments and/or returning them.

questions.prompt:
```js
console.log([1, 2, 3].map((n) => n * 2));
```
What prints?
questions.explanation: `map` returns a new array with each element transformed by the callback, keeping the same length as the input.

questions.prompt:
```js
console.log(["a", "", "b", ""].filter((s) => s !== ""));
```
What is the length of the printed array?
questions.explanation: `filter` keeps only elements where the predicate is truthy. Only `"a"` and `"b"` pass, so the result has length 2.

questions.prompt: After `const result = [1, 2, 3].map((n) => n * 2);`, what is the original array?
questions.explanation: `map` never mutates the array it is called on — it always returns a brand-new array.

questions.prompt: Can the result of `filter` be shorter than the input array?

options.text: No, `filter` always returns the same length as the input
Yes, only elements where the predicate returns truthy are kept
No, `filter` throws if any element is removed
Only if the input array is empty

questions.explanation: Unlike `map`, `filter` can shrink the array — every element that fails the predicate is dropped from the result.
`pipeline` composes the steps in order: trim first ("hi"), then uppercase ("HI"). `pipeline` itself is higher-order — it takes functions and returns one.

quizzes.title: Prototype Chain Check
quizzes.description: Predict own vs inherited property lookups via Object.create, Object.assign, in, and Object.hasOwn.

questions.explanation: `greet` lives on `parent`, not directly on `child`. `Object.hasOwn` only reports own properties, so it returns `false`.

questions.prompt: Using the same `child`, what does `"greet" in child` print?
questions.explanation: The `in` operator checks the entire prototype chain, so it finds `greet` on `parent` and reports `true`.

options.text: `true` — assign copies properties directly onto the target

questions.explanation: `Object.assign(target, source)` copies `source`'s properties as own properties onto `target`. `b` becomes an own property of `child`.

questions.prompt: For the same `child` (prototype has `a`, own property `b`), what does `Object.hasOwn(child, "a")` print?
questions.explanation: `a` is only reachable through the prototype (`{ a: 1 }`), not copied onto `child` — so it is not an own property.

questions.prompt: What does `"c" in child` print when `child` has no `c` on itself or on its prototype?
questions.explanation: If a key is not found anywhere in the prototype chain (own or inherited), `in` reports `false`.

questions.prompt: Which pair of checks correctly distinguishes "own" from "inherited" for a given key on an object?

options.text: `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` for own, and `key in obj` (when hasOwn is false) for inherited

questions.explanation: Check `Object.hasOwn` first for own properties; if that is false but `key in obj` is true, the property is inherited from the prototype chain.

quizzes.title: ES6 Modules Check
quizzes.description: Classify export/import statements as default or named.

questions.prompt: `export default function main() {}` is which kind of export?
questions.explanation: `export default` marks the module's single default export, whatever follows it (function, class, expression).

questions.prompt: `export { helper, util };` is which kind of export?
questions.explanation: Curly-brace `export { X }` declares one or more named exports — the importing side must use matching names in braces.

questions.prompt: `export const PI = 3.14;` is which kind of export?

options.text: Default export, because there's only one value
Named export — same import style as `export { PI }`

questions.explanation: `export const X`, `export let X`, `export function X`, and `export { X }` are all named exports — a module can have many of these.

questions.prompt: `import config from "./config.js";` (no curly braces) targets which kind of export?
questions.explanation: An import with no braces always targets the default export — the local name (`config`) can be anything, since there is only one default per module.

questions.prompt: `import { helper } from "./utils.js";` (with curly braces) targets which kind of export?

options.text: Nothing — braces are only for destructuring objects

questions.explanation: Braces on import always target a named export — the name inside the braces must match the exported name exactly (unless aliased with `as`).

questions.prompt: Can a single module have both a default export and named exports?

options.text: No, a module can only export one thing total
Yes — one default export plus any number of named exports
Yes, but only if they have the same name
No, default and named exports must live in separate files

questions.explanation: A module may have at most one default export, and separately, as many named exports as needed — they coexist in the same file.

`count` is captured by reference inside the closure, so each `inc()` call mutates the same private variable that `get()` later reads.

`filter` keeps only the elements where the callback returns a truthy value, producing a new (possibly shorter) array — here the two non-empty strings.

quizzes.title: Big-O Complexity Check
quizzes.description: Predict the time complexity of common loop shapes.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of a single loop that iterates over every element of an array once?
questions.explanation: One pass over `n` elements means the work grows linearly with `n` — that's `O(n)`.

questions.prompt: A function has a loop inside another loop, both running over the same array. What is its complexity?
questions.explanation: Nested loops over the same input multiply: `n` iterations of the outer loop, each running `n` iterations of the inner loop, gives `O(n^2)`.

questions.prompt: Binary search on a sorted array halves the remaining range on every step. What is its complexity?
questions.explanation: Halving the search range each step means the number of steps grows with `log n`, not `n`.

questions.prompt: A function returns `arr[0]` with no loop and no recursion. What is its complexity?
questions.explanation: No loop and a fixed number of operations means the work does not grow with input size — that's `O(1)`, constant time.

questions.prompt: A function does `3n + 100` operations for an input of size `n`. What is its Big-O complexity?
questions.explanation: Big-O drops constant factors and lower-order terms; `3n + 100` still grows linearly, so it is classified as `O(n)`.

questions.prompt: As `n` doubles, which complexity class sees its operation count roughly quadruple?
questions.explanation: For `O(n^2)`, doubling `n` means `(2n)^2 = 4n^2` — roughly four times the work, unlike `O(n)` which only doubles.

quizzes.title: Two Pointers and Sliding Window Check
quizzes.description: Predict pointer movement and complexity for two-pointer and sliding-window patterns.

questions.prompt: In the two-pointer `twoSum` on a sorted array, if `sortedArr[left] + sortedArr[right] < target`, what should happen next?

options.text: Move `left` one step right (increase the sum)
Move `right` one step left (decrease the sum)
Move both pointers to the middle

questions.explanation: If the sum is too small, you need a bigger value; moving `left` right on a sorted array increases the sum.

questions.prompt: Why does the sorted two-pointer approach run in `O(n)` instead of `O(n^2)`?

options.text: Because it uses recursion instead of loops
Because each pointer moves at most `n` times total, instead of re-checking every pair
Because it sorts the array first, which is free
Because JavaScript arrays are hash maps internally

questions.explanation: Each pointer only moves forward (or backward) and never revisits a position, bounding total pointer movement to `O(n)` instead of checking all `n^2` pairs.

questions.prompt: In the sliding window for longest unique substring, when do you shrink the window from the left?

options.text: Every single iteration, regardless of content
When the character at `right` is already in the current window
Only when the window reaches the end of the string

questions.explanation: The window shrinks from the left only when a duplicate character is found, removing characters until the duplicate is gone.

questions.prompt: Why is it safe to shrink the sliding window from the left without missing a better answer?

options.text: Because the window is always sorted
Because any smaller window contained in the current one was already considered as `best` was updated
It is not safe — this is a bug in the pattern

questions.explanation: As `right` advances, `best` is updated on every valid window, so shrinking from the left never discards an answer better than what has already been recorded.

questions.prompt: Two pointers moving from each end toward the middle is most directly applicable when the array is:

options.text: Sorted, so comparing the sum to the target tells you which pointer to move
A linked list, not an array
Guaranteed to have no valid answer

questions.explanation: The sorted order is what makes the pointer decision (move left vs. move right) correct — without it, moving a pointer could skip the answer.

questions.prompt: What is the overall time complexity of the sliding window `longestUnique` function?

options.text: `O(n)`, because `left` and `right` together make at most `2n` moves

questions.explanation: Even though there's a nested `while`, `left` can only advance up to `n` times total across the whole run, so the combined work is still `O(n)`.

quizzes.title: BFS and DFS Check
quizzes.description: Predict traversal order and the queue-vs-stack difference between BFS and DFS.

questions.prompt: Which data structure does BFS use to decide which node to visit next?
questions.explanation: BFS uses a queue: nodes are dequeued in the same order they were enqueued (FIFO), which produces level-by-level order.

questions.prompt: For adjacency list `[[1, 2], [3], [3], []]` starting at node `0`, what is the BFS visit order?
questions.explanation: BFS visits `0` first, enqueues `1` and `2` (its direct neighbors), then dequeues `1`, enqueues `3`, then dequeues `2` (already visited `3` is skipped), then dequeues `3` — giving `0, 1, 2, 3`.

questions.prompt: Why is BFS guaranteed to find the shortest path in an unweighted graph?

options.text: It visits nodes in alphabetical order
It visits all nodes at distance `k` before any node at distance `k+1`
It uses recursion, which is always optimal
It sorts edges by weight first

questions.explanation: BFS explores level by level (by number of edges from the start), so the first time it reaches a node is guaranteed to be via the fewest edges.

questions.prompt: What is the key structural difference between the BFS and DFS implementations shown in the lesson?

options.text: BFS uses `queue.shift()` (FIFO); DFS uses `stack.pop()` (LIFO) — everything else is the same
DFS does not need a `visited` set
BFS only works on trees, not graphs
DFS always runs faster than BFS

questions.explanation: Both implementations are structurally identical except for one operation: dequeue (FIFO) for BFS vs. pop (LIFO) for DFS.

questions.prompt: Why do both BFS and DFS mark a node as visited before or when adding it to the queue/stack?

options.text: To make the output alphabetically sorted
To avoid revisiting nodes and looping forever on a graph with cycles
It is optional and only affects performance slightly
To reduce memory usage of the adjacency list

questions.explanation: Without tracking visited nodes, a graph with a cycle would cause the traversal to revisit the same nodes forever.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of both BFS and DFS on a graph with `V` vertices and `E` edges?
questions.explanation: Every vertex is visited once and every edge is examined once, giving `O(V + E)` for both traversals.

quizzes.title: Cycle Detection Check
quizzes.description: Predict Floyd's tortoise-and-hare behavior on next-pointer chains.

questions.prompt: In Floyd's algorithm, how many steps does the `fast` pointer take for every one step of `slow`?

options.text: It depends on the list length

questions.explanation: `fast` always moves two steps (`next[next[fast]]`) while `slow` moves one step (`next[slow]`) — the differing speed is what causes them to meet inside a cycle.

questions.prompt: For `next = [1, 2, 3, 1]` starting at index `0` (chain `0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 1 -> ...`), does `hasCycle` return `true` or `false`?

options.text: `true` — `slow` and `fast` eventually land on the same index

questions.explanation: The chain loops back to index `1`, so it has a cycle. Because `fast` never reaches `-1` (it just keeps looping), `slow` and `fast` are guaranteed to meet.

questions.prompt: For `next = [1, 2, -1]` starting at index `0` (chain `0 -> 1 -> 2 -> end`), what happens?

options.text: It throws because `fast` goes out of bounds

questions.explanation: The chain ends cleanly (no cycle). Since the loop condition checks `fast !== -1 && next[fast] !== -1`, it stops before dereferencing an invalid index, and returns `false`.

questions.prompt: Compared to the hash-set approach, what does Floyd's tortoise-and-hare trade away to save memory?

options.text: It uses two pointers instead of a `Set`, still `O(n)` time but `O(1)` extra space
It only works on arrays, not linked lists
It cannot detect cycles at all, only measure length

questions.explanation: Floyd's algorithm keeps the same `O(n)` time complexity as the hash-set version but uses `O(1)` extra space instead of `O(n)` for a `Set`.

questions.prompt: For `next = [2, 2, 2]` starting at index `0`, is there a cycle?

options.text: Yes — node `2` points to itself, forming a self-loop
It depends on the starting index

questions.explanation: `0 -> 2 -> 2 -> 2 -> ...` — node `2`'s `next` points to itself, which is a valid (and detectable) cycle even though it involves just one node looping.

questions.prompt: Does a 'cycle' in this context require looping back to the very first node visited?

options.text: Yes, only a loop back to the start counts
No — any node's `next` chain revisiting an earlier node counts as a cycle
Yes, but only for arrays of even length
No — a cycle must visit every node in the list

questions.explanation: A cycle exists whenever the chain of `next` pointers revisits any node already seen, not necessarily the very first one — as in `0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 1 -> ...`.

quizzes.title: Dynamic Programming Check
quizzes.description: Predict DP table values and identify overlapping subproblems vs. optimal substructure.

questions.prompt: What two properties must a problem have for Dynamic Programming to apply?

options.text: Sorted input and a single loop
A graph structure and no cycles

questions.explanation: DP exploits overlapping subproblems (the same smaller problem recurs) combined with optimal substructure (the answer is built from smaller answers).

questions.prompt: Why is `waysNaive(n)` exponential time?

options.text: Because it uses a `for` loop internally
Because it recomputes the same subproblems (like `ways(3)`) many times across different recursive branches
Because JavaScript recursion is always slow
Because it uses an array instead of a table

questions.explanation: Without memoization or a table, each call branches into two more calls, and the same smaller subproblem gets solved repeatedly — this is the overlapping-subproblems cost.

questions.prompt: In `waysDP`, what does `table[i] = table[i - 1] + table[i - 2]` represent?

options.text: The number of ways to reach step `i`, built from the already-computed ways to reach `i-1` and `i-2`
The total number of steps taken so far

questions.explanation: The last step taken to reach `i` was either a single step from `i-1` or a double step from `i-2` — summing those two already-solved subproblems gives `ways(i)`.

questions.prompt: What is `waysDP(4)` given `table[0] = 1` and `table[1] = 1`?
What is the time complexity of `waysDP(n)` compared to `waysNaive(n)`?
questions.explanation: `waysDP` fills each subproblem once in a single pass (`O(n)`); `waysNaive` re-solves overlapping subproblems across an exponentially branching call tree (`O(2^n)`).

questions.prompt: Does DP change *what* is computed compared to the naive recursive formula, or *how* it is computed?

options.text: It changes what is computed — DP uses a different recurrence
It changes how it is computed — the same recurrence is filled bottom-up and reused instead of recomputed
It changes neither; DP is purely a naming convention

questions.explanation: The recurrence `ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2)` is identical in both versions; DP only changes the computation strategy from repeated recursive calls to a single bottom-up table fill.

quizzes.title: Data Structures and Algorithms Multiple Choice

questions.prompt: Binary search halves the remaining range on every iteration. What is its time complexity?
questions.explanation: Halving the search range each step means the number of steps grows by only one when n doubles — that is the definition of O(log n).

questions.prompt: For `twoSum(sortedArr, target)` using the two-pointer technique on a SORTED array, what do you do when `sortedArr[left] + sortedArr[right] < target`?

options.text: Move `left` one step to the right to increase the sum
Move `right` one step to the left to decrease the sum
Restart both pointers from the ends

questions.explanation: When the current sum is too small, the only way to increase it (on a sorted array) is to move the left pointer right, since every value from that point on is greater or equal.

questions.prompt: Why does the two-pointer / sliding window technique reduce a nested-loop O(n²) solution to O(n)?

options.text: Each pointer moves in only one direction and makes at most n moves total, so no pair or window is re-examined from scratch
It sorts the array first, which is always free
It uses recursion instead of loops, which is inherently faster
It only works on arrays with fewer than 100 elements

questions.explanation: Because each pointer only advances (never backtracks), the total work across the whole pass is bounded by n moves per pointer, giving O(n) instead of checking every pair.

options.text: BFS uses a FIFO queue (`shift`); DFS uses a LIFO stack (`pop`) — everything else is the same
BFS uses recursion; DFS never uses recursion
DFS always runs faster than BFS on the same graph
BFS cannot be used on graphs with cycles

questions.prompt: In an unweighted graph, which traversal is guaranteed to find the shortest path (fewest edges) from a start node?

options.text: BFS, because it explores level by level
DFS, because it explores as deep as possible first
Only Dijkstra's algorithm can do this

questions.explanation: BFS visits all direct neighbors before any of their neighbors (level by level), which is exactly why it finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph.

questions.prompt: Floyd's tortoise and hare algorithm detects a cycle in a linked list using two pointers moving at different speeds. What is its space complexity, and why is that an advantage over a hash-set approach?

options.text: O(1) extra space, because it only tracks two pointers instead of storing every visited node
O(n) extra space, same as the hash-set approach
O(log n) extra space, because it halves the list each step
O(n²) extra space, because it compares every pair of nodes

questions.explanation: Floyd's algorithm trades the hash-set's O(n) memory for two pointers (`slow`/`fast`), achieving O(1) extra space while still running in O(n) time.

questions.prompt: What two properties must a problem have for dynamic programming to help?

options.text: A sorted input and a single loop
A graph structure and a queue

questions.explanation: DP applies when the same smaller subproblem recurs (overlapping subproblems) and the best overall answer is built from the best answers to smaller pieces (optimal substructure).
